subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease with delayed presentation past day 10
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3 year old boy in the general paediatric ward. He was admitted six hours ago from a rural general practice with fever for the last eleven days, widespread red rash over his trunk that began on day three, cracked lips, red eyes without discharge, and a swollen left neck lump that his mother says has been there for a week.

His mother reports his hands and feet were puffy and pink for four days last week and the skin is now peeling around his fingertips. There was no overseas travel, no unwell contacts, and no antibiotic use. Blood cultures taken on admission are negative at 24 hours.

An echocardiogram performed this morning reports normal coronary arteries with no ectasia and no pericardial effusion, and normal biventricular function.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, dry cracked lips with strawberry tongue, polymorphous truncal rash, 2.5 cm left anterior cervical lymph node, peeling skin at fingertips
data_table.Investigations: CRP 158 mg/L (<5), platelets 612 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 78 U/L (<40), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), urine white cells present without organisms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Withhold IVIG because presentation is past day ten and the echocardiogram is normal, and observe for defervescence
options.rationale: Fulfilment of four principal criteria with persistent inflammation (CRP 158, platelets 612, hyponatraemia, hypoalbuminaemia) meets the AHA definition of Kawasaki disease presenting late. IVIG is still indicated beyond day 10 when inflammatory markers are elevated OR coronary changes are present, because it lowers aneurysm risk even in the sub-acute phase. Withholding therapy exposes the child to progressive coronary injury. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Discharge home on ibuprofen for symptom control with paediatric outpatient review in two weeks and a repeat echocardiogram at six weeks
options.rationale: Discharge on a non-steroidal without immunomodulation abandons the disease-modifying window entirely. Ibuprofen does not treat vasculitis and worsens the risk profile if aspirin is later required. Inpatient IVIG plus aspirin is the standard of care. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Change antibiotics to IV ceftriaxone monotherapy and request repeat blood cultures and a monospot before considering further immunomodulation
options.rationale: The clinical pattern is not bacterial sepsis nor EBV (no exudative pharyngitis, no splenomegaly, negative cultures at 24 hours). Antibiotic escalation delays IVIG. Kawasaki disease is a clinical diagnosis and infectious workup should not defer treatment when criteria are met. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse as first line, and hold IVIG until steroid response is assessed at 48 hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroids in Kawasaki disease are adjunctive for predicted IVIG resistance or for genuine IVIG failure (persistent fever 36 hours after first infusion), not as a first-line replacement for IVIG. Steroid monotherapy leaves the coronary risk unaddressed. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)

options.text: Give a single dose of IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 12 hours plus high dose aspirin, and repeat echocardiogram at two and six weeks
options.rationale: This child fulfils four of the five principal criteria (rash, conjunctivitis, mucous membrane changes, extremity changes, cervical adenopathy >1.5 cm) with persistent fever and strongly elevated inflammatory markers past day 10; RCH and AHA both recommend IVIG plus aspirin in the sub-acute phase provided CRP or coronary artery changes remain. Serial echocardiography detects late aneurysm formation. (Source: RCH CPG: Kawasaki disease)
source_refs: American Heart Association Kawasaki disease scientific statement

explanation.summary: Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of early childhood; the coronary arteries are the principal target and untreated disease carries a 25% risk of aneurysm formation, falling to under 5% with timely IVIG. RCH and the American Heart Association both treat presentations beyond day 10 with IVIG plus aspirin when systemic inflammation persists (CRP raised, ESR raised, platelets rising, hypoalbuminaemia, sterile pyuria) or when the echocardiogram shows coronary changes. Aspirin is used at anti-inflammatory dose while febrile then reduced to antiplatelet dose for six to eight weeks or until inflammatory markers normalise. Follow-up echocardiography at two and six weeks catches late aneurysm development.
key_points: Four of five principal criteria plus fever meet clinical Kawasaki diagnosis; incomplete Kawasaki uses a supplementary lab algorithm.
IVIG 2 g/kg reduces coronary aneurysm risk from roughly 25% to under 5%.
Late-presenting Kawasaki (after day 10) still receives IVIG if CRP raised or coronaries abnormal.
IVIG resistance (fever >36 hours after infusion) is the trigger for adjunctive steroids or infliximab.
Aspirin is used at anti-inflammatory then antiplatelet dose and is one of the paediatric exceptions to the Reye syndrome caution.
explanation.pearls: Sterile pyuria plus a strawberry tongue plus a platelet count above 450 x10^9/L in a persistently febrile toddler flips the differential from viral exanthem toward Kawasaki disease before the classic extremity peeling appears.

sources.label: American Heart Association Kawasaki disease scientific statement

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in an at-risk newborn
stem:
You are the paediatric intern reviewing a 2 hour old term male infant on the postnatal ward. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 plus 4 weeks to a mother with insulin-treated gestational diabetes. Birth weight was 4420 g (above the 97th centile). Apgars were 9 and 9.

The mother is keen to exclusively breastfeed. The baby has fed at the breast for 15 minutes with a shallow latch and is now quiet and pink with normal tone. The bedside heel-prick pre-feed blood glucose is 1.9 mmol/L (target >=2.6 in the first 24 hours). Cord gases were normal and there is no respiratory distress.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148 /min, respiratory rate 44 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC in an open cot with skin-to-skin available
data_table.Examination: Large for gestational age, alert and quiet, normal tone, no jitteriness, no cyanosis, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Feeding: One breastfeed attempted with shallow latch, no formula or expressed breast milk given, mother has colostrum available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose intravenous bolus and admit to the special care nursery for continuous glucose monitoring
options.rationale: IV dextrose bolus is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia OR persistently low glucose despite oral or buccal glucose gel measures. An asymptomatic first low reading at 1.9 mmol/L is treated first with oral 40% glucose gel and a feed, per RCH and Australasian pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Send serum insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ammonia, and lactate for a critical hypoglycaemia screen before any further intervention
options.rationale: A hyperinsulinism screen is triggered by hypoglycaemia persisting beyond 48 hours, requiring glucose infusion rates above 8 mg/kg/min, or occurring outside a recognised risk category. It is not the first response to a single mildly low reading in an infant of a diabetic mother. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Give 30 mL/kg of formula immediately via bottle and defer any further blood glucose testing for six hours if the baby settles
options.rationale: A 30 mL/kg formula bolus at 2 hours of life is a supra-physiological volume and undermines breastfeeding without addressing the immediate metabolic risk any better than gel plus feed. Testing intervals are pre-feed at 2, 4, 6, 12, 24 hours for infants of diabetic mothers, not at a six-hour gap. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Reassure the parents that a single low reading at two hours is a normal physiological nadir, avoid intervention, and repeat the glucose at four hours
options.rationale: The physiological glucose nadir in healthy term babies is around 1 hour of life; a value of 1.9 mmol/L at 2 hours in an infant of a diabetic mother is below the RCH intervention threshold of 2.6 mmol/L and requires active management, not observation. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Apply 200 mg/kg of 40% dextrose gel to the buccal mucosa, support a further breastfeed with expressed colostrum top-up, and recheck blood glucose in 30 minutes
options.rationale: The Sugar Babies/HYPO protocol adopted by RCH treats asymptomatic hypoglycaemia below 2.6 mmol/L in at-risk infants with 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) of 40% buccal dextrose gel plus a supported feed, then rechecks the level 30 minutes after the feed. This avoids unnecessary separation and preserves breastfeeding. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal hypoglycaemia)
source_refs: Sugar Babies (Harris 2013) buccal dextrose gel trial

explanation.summary: Neonatal hypoglycaemia is managed on a stepped pathway that keeps the mother-baby dyad together where possible. RCH defines a target of at least 2.6 mmol/L pre-feed from 2 hours of age in at-risk infants: infants of diabetic mothers, small or large for gestational age, preterm 35-37 weeks, and those with perinatal stress. Asymptomatic first low readings are treated with buccal 40% dextrose gel at 200 mg/kg plus a supported breastfeed, with recheck 30 minutes after the feed. Failure of two gel-and-feed cycles, symptomatic hypoglycaemia, or a glucose under 1.5 mmol/L escalates to IV dextrose and special-care admission with a target glucose infusion rate that keeps the infant euglycaemic.
key_points: At-risk infants (IDM, LGA, SGA, late preterm, perinatal stress) get pre-feed BSL at 2, 4, 6, 12, 24 hours.
First-line treatment for asymptomatic BSL <2.6 mmol/L is 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) of 40% dextrose gel plus a feed.
Recheck BSL 30 minutes after the feed; if still low, repeat gel plus feed once before IV dextrose.
Symptomatic hypoglycaemia or BSL <1.5 mmol/L bypasses gel and goes straight to IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg then infusion.
Persistent hypoglycaemia beyond 48 hours or GIR >8 mg/kg/min triggers a hyperinsulinism screen.
explanation.pearls: Buccal 40% dextrose gel dosed at 200 mg/kg keeps the mother and baby together and reduces NICU admission for hypoglycaemia by about 40% in the Sugar Babies trial - remember 0.5 mL/kg of 40% gel.

sources.label: Sugar Babies (Harris 2013) buccal dextrose gel trial

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia from excess cow's milk intake
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing an 18 month old girl brought in by her father who is worried she looks pale. She was born at term with an uneventful pregnancy, has never travelled overseas, and has no family history of haemoglobinopathy or bleeding disorder. Her diet consists of about 900 mL of full-cream cow's milk daily from a bottle, plus small amounts of white bread, plain rice and biscuits; she refuses meat, egg and green vegetables.

Her father has not noticed any dark stools, epistaxis, bruising or bleeding gums. She was fully breastfed until twelve months and reached her motor milestones on time. On examination she is on the 50th centile for weight and height, pale conjunctivae, no jaundice, no scleral icterus, no organomegaly and no lymphadenopathy.

Full blood count shows a microcytic anaemia; the pathologist has held the sample for iron studies.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Full blood count: Haemoglobin 82 g/L (110-140), MCV 62 fL (75-87), MCH 20 pg (25-33), red cell count 4.5 x10^12/L (3.9-5.3), platelets 468 x10^9/L (150-400), white cells 8.2 x10^9/L (5-15)
data_table.Blood film: Microcytic hypochromic red cells with anisopoikilocytosis, no basophilic stippling, no target cells

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her workup and management?

options.text: Start oral ferrous sulfate at 3 mg/kg elemental iron daily, reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL per day, and send ferritin and coeliac serology today
options.rationale: The clinical picture (excess milk intake, meat refusal, microcytic hypochromic anaemia without haemolysis or bleeding) is classic dietary iron deficiency. RCH treats with 3-6 mg/kg elemental iron daily and reduces cow's milk to below 500 mL/day. Coeliac serology (transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA) is co-ordered because coeliac disease is a common co-cause of iron deficiency in toddlers. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Arrange an urgent bone marrow biopsy through the paediatric haematology day unit before commencing any oral iron therapy for this toddler
options.rationale: Bone marrow biopsy is reserved for suspected marrow failure, refractory anaemia after adequate iron replacement, or when the blood film and history do not fit a common cause. Dietary iron deficiency in an otherwise well toddler does not warrant an invasive procedure as a first step. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Arrange an intravenous iron carboxymaltose infusion as first-line treatment given the degree of the microcytic anaemia at presentation today
options.rationale: IV iron in children under five is reserved for oral iron intolerance, malabsorption (coeliac, IBD), or ongoing losses that outstrip oral replacement. A well toddler with dietary iron deficiency will respond to oral iron; ferric carboxymaltose is not licensed under one year and is second line under five. (Source: AMH Children's Dosing Companion)

options.text: Request haemoglobin electrophoresis first and defer iron therapy until beta thalassaemia trait has been definitively excluded on the panel
options.rationale: The presentation strongly favours iron deficiency (dietary history, low MCH, high red cell distribution width, no family history of haemoglobinopathy). Iron replacement should not be delayed pending electrophoresis, though electrophoresis is legitimate if the response to iron is inadequate at eight weeks. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Prescribe an over-the-counter paediatric multivitamin containing 4 mg of iron once daily and review the full blood count in six months' time
options.rationale: A multivitamin containing 4 mg of iron delivers approximately one-fifth of the therapeutic dose required and will not correct clinical anaemia in a reasonable timeframe. Six-month review of a haemoglobin of 82 g/L delays diagnosis of the roughly 20% of iron-deficient toddlers who have an underlying malabsorptive cause. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia is the commonest paediatric anaemia in Australia, peaking between nine months and three years when rapid growth outstrips a milk-heavy diet with limited iron intake. Excess cow's milk (>500 mL/day) both displaces iron-rich foods and causes occult gut blood loss through non-IgE cow's milk protein enteropathy in some children. Assessment includes an iron panel with ferritin (an acute phase reactant that may be falsely normal), coeliac serology, and dietary counselling. Oral ferrous sulfate 3-6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron is first line; expect a haemoglobin rise of about 10 g/L per fortnight and a reticulocyte response within a week. Continue treatment for three months beyond haemoglobin normalisation to replenish stores.
key_points: Cap cow's milk at 500 mL/day in toddlers to prevent iron deficiency.
First-line oral iron dose is 3-6 mg/kg/day of elemental iron; ferrous sulfate 30 mg = 6 mg elemental.
Co-order coeliac serology because coeliac disease is a common cause of refractory iron deficiency.
Expect Hb rise of about 10 g/L per fortnight; failure to respond triggers investigation for malabsorption or loss.
Continue oral iron for three months after Hb normalises to refill stores.
explanation.pearls: In a well-appearing toddler with dietary iron deficiency, transferrin saturation below 16% and ferritin below 15 microg/L confirm the diagnosis; a rise in reticulocyte count within seven days of starting ferrous sulfate proves the therapy is working before the haemoglobin has moved.

subtopic_detail: Bruising in a non-mobile infant and mandatory reporting
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan emergency department. A 4 month old boy is brought in by his mother because of a bruise on his left cheek. She says the baby was strapped into his bouncer on the lounge carpet and the family cat jumped over him; she thinks the cat's paw caught his face.

The infant is exclusively breastfed, born at term, and has met developmental milestones for his age. He is not rolling and cannot sit unsupported. There is no family history of bleeding disorder, no antenatal concerns, and no previous hospital presentations recorded on the state-wide record.

On examination he is alert and interactive with his mother. There is a 2 cm x 1 cm blue-purple bruise over the left zygoma without abrasion. Fundoscopy is normal. The rest of the skin survey shows a linear 1 cm bruise on the left pinna. Full blood count, coagulation profile and blood film are all within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Skin survey: Left zygomatic bruise 2 cm x 1 cm; left pinna 1 cm linear bruise; no other bruises, no burns, no bite marks, no torn frenulum
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, prothrombin ratio 1.0, activated partial thromboplastin time 32 s (25-35), fibrinogen 3.1 g/L (2-4)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother that the mechanism is plausible, arrange general practice review in one week, and discharge the infant home without further investigation
options.rationale: Bruising in a pre-mobile infant carries a strong statistical association with inflicted injury regardless of the explanation offered, because the mechanisms available to an infant who cannot roll are extremely limited. Discharge without a full skeletal survey and child protection referral misses occult fractures and abusive head trauma. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Admit for a full skeletal survey, urgent MRI brain, and a same-shift referral to the child protection unit with a mandatory report to the statutory child protection agency
options.rationale: Any bruise in a non-mobile infant is a sentinel injury: TEN-4 FACESp screening puts this in the highest concern category (face and ear bruising, under 4 months). RCH mandates full skeletal survey, neuroimaging for abusive head trauma, ophthalmology fundoscopy, and same-day involvement of the hospital child protection team plus a mandatory report to statutory services. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)
source_refs: TEN-4 FACESp bruising clinical decision rule

options.text: Request only a coagulation panel plus von Willebrand studies before deciding whether further investigation for inflicted injury is needed
options.rationale: Bleeding disorders should be excluded but do not replace child protection assessment. Coagulation screening runs in parallel with skeletal survey, neuroimaging and social work involvement, not instead of them. Sequential single-track workup delays safeguarding decisions. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Photograph the bruises for the medical record, discharge home with an information leaflet on infant bruising, and request a home visit by the child health nurse within 48 hours
options.rationale: Photodocumentation is important but not sufficient. Discharging a pre-mobile infant with unexplained bruising home before completing the skeletal survey and safeguarding pathway exposes the child to further injury; the child health nurse cannot substitute for the paediatric child protection team. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Order a plain radiograph of the skull and left ribs, and if normal manage as accidental injury per the mother's account without notifying statutory services
options.rationale: A limited two-view series misses the classic metaphyseal lesions, posterior rib fractures, and healing fractures that a full 21-view skeletal survey detects. Statutory notification is mandatory for reasonable suspicion regardless of imaging results in every Australian jurisdiction. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: The mantra 'those who don't cruise rarely bruise' captures the epidemiology: bruising in an infant who cannot yet mobilise (roll, cruise, walk) is exceptional in accidental injury and highly predictive of inflicted trauma. The TEN-4 FACESp decision rule flags bruising to the Trunk, Ear, Neck in any child under four years, Face, Angle of jaw, Cheek, Eyelid or Subconjunctivae, or Patterned bruising, and any bruise in a pre-cruiser as a sentinel injury requiring evaluation. Standard RCH workup includes full skeletal survey (repeated at 2 weeks for equivocal findings), MRI brain, dilated fundoscopy, coagulation and full blood count, and same-day involvement of the paediatric child protection team. Mandatory reporting to the statutory child protection agency is triggered by reasonable belief of harm, not diagnostic certainty.
key_points: Pre-mobile infant bruising is a sentinel injury for abusive head trauma and occult fracture.
TEN-4 FACESp flags Torso, Ear, Neck (under 4 years); Face, Angle jaw, Cheek, Eyelid, Subconjunctivae; Patterned; and pre-cruisers.
Full skeletal survey (21 views) not a limited two-view study; consider a repeat at 2 weeks.
MRI brain is preferred over CT for abusive head trauma; dilated fundoscopy for retinal haemorrhages.
Mandatory reporting is triggered by reasonable belief, not certainty; runs in parallel with medical workup.
explanation.pearls: A bruise on the ear or the cheek of an infant under 4 months old carries a positive predictive value for inflicted injury above 90% in TEN-4 FACESp derivation cohorts; a full skeletal survey plus MRI brain the same day is standard of care regardless of the explanation offered.

sources.label: TEN-4 FACESp bruising clinical decision rule

subtopic_detail: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and biliary atresia workup
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5 week old exclusively breastfed girl referred by her general practitioner for prolonged jaundice. She was born at term by uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Her weight is tracking along the 25th centile. Her mother reports that stool has been pale for about ten days and that her urine has been dark coloured and staining the nappy for the last week.

There is no family history of liver or metabolic disease. She had a normal newborn screening blood spot. The mother tolerated a routine antenatal package and had a normal 20 week anomaly scan.

On examination she is alert with a soft cry, mildly icteric sclerae, a 2 cm smooth liver edge and no splenomegaly. There is no bruising. The direct antiglobulin test is negative and blood groups are matched with the mother.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Bilirubin: Total bilirubin 152 micromol/L (<20), conjugated (direct) fraction 68 micromol/L (<20)
data_table.Liver panel: ALT 92 U/L (<40), AST 118 U/L (<40), GGT 385 U/L (<50), ALP 620 U/L, albumin 34 g/L (35-50), INR 1.1
data_table.Other: Full blood count within normal limits, thyroid function within normal limits, urine reducing substances negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Advise that breast milk jaundice can persist to 12 weeks, arrange a repeat total bilirubin in two weeks, and reassure the mother that no further action is needed
options.rationale: Breast milk jaundice is UNCONJUGATED. A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L (or above 20% of total) is always pathological in infancy and cannot be attributed to breastfeeding. Delayed workup misses the Kasai-portoenterostomy window for biliary atresia. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Start phototherapy at hospital admission and check response with a total serum bilirubin at 24 hours before deciding whether further investigation is required
options.rationale: Phototherapy converts unconjugated bilirubin to water-soluble isomers; it does not treat conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and can cause bronze baby syndrome in the presence of a significant direct fraction. It also anchors decision-making on the wrong pathway. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Admit for urgent hepatology consultation with hepatobiliary ultrasound, same-week HIDA scan and specialist-guided liver biopsy to expedite the biliary atresia workup
options.rationale: A conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L with pale stool and dark urine in an infant is biliary atresia until proven otherwise. Kasai portoenterostomy performed before 60 days of life gives the best long-term native-liver survival, so admit, involve paediatric hepatology, and expedite the triple workup of ultrasound, HIDA and liver biopsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)
source_refs: GESA and Liver Foundation Australia biliary atresia pathway

options.text: Advise a two-week trial of formula feeding and repeat both total and conjugated bilirubin at the end of the trial to distinguish breast milk from other causes
options.rationale: A milk-swap trial is only relevant to distinguishing breast milk unconjugated jaundice; it has no role once the conjugated fraction is elevated. Two weeks of delay in biliary atresia crosses the critical 60-day surgical window. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Request urine culture for urinary tract infection and thyroid stimulating hormone first, with hepatology referral only if these first-line tests are unremarkable
options.rationale: UTI and hypothyroidism are recognised causes of prolonged UNCONJUGATED jaundice. Neither typically produces a conjugated fraction of 68 micromol/L with pale stools. Sequential ruling out of these before hepatology referral delays the surgical window for biliary atresia. (Source: RCH CPG: Prolonged neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Any jaundice persisting beyond 14 days in a term infant (21 days in a preterm) must have a split bilirubin done. A conjugated fraction above 20 micromol/L, or above 20% of the total, is always pathological. The differential includes biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, neonatal hepatitis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, cystic fibrosis, TORCH infection, metabolic disorders and parenteral nutrition associated cholestasis. Biliary atresia is the not-to-miss diagnosis because Kasai portoenterostomy performed before 60 days of life gives the best native-liver survival; every week of delay after that meaningfully worsens outcomes. Standard workup pairs ultrasound (looking for the 'triangular cord sign' and absent gallbladder) with hepatobiliary scintigraphy (HIDA) after phenobarbitone priming and, when indicated, liver biopsy plus intraoperative cholangiogram.
key_points: Split bilirubin is mandatory for jaundice persisting beyond 14 days (21 days preterm).
Conjugated bilirubin above 20 micromol/L or above 20% of total is pathological.
Pale stool plus dark urine is biliary atresia until proven otherwise.
Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days of life optimises native-liver survival.
Phototherapy has no role and can cause bronze baby syndrome when conjugated fraction is high.
explanation.pearls: Any breastfed baby still jaundiced at two weeks needs a split bilirubin; a direct fraction of 68 micromol/L with pale stools mandates same-week ultrasound and hepatology referral because Kasai portoenterostomy done inside the 60-day window doubles the 10-year native-liver survival.

sources.label: GESA and Liver Foundation Australia biliary atresia pathway

subtopic_detail: Hemiplegic migraine masquerading as acute ischaemic stroke
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 10 year old girl in the emergency department. She woke this morning with a headache behind her right eye, tingling of the left side of her lips and left hand, and then developed left arm weakness that reached its worst at about 45 minutes and has been present for two hours.

Her mother has migraine with aura and her maternal aunt has had similar episodes since childhood. There is no history of head trauma, cardiac disease, sickle cell disease, prior thrombotic event or oral contraceptive use. Six months ago she had a similar left-sided episode that resolved fully over four hours and was labelled a probable migraine variant.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable and speaks in slow, dysarthric sentences. There is 3/5 power in the left arm and 4/5 in the left leg with brisk reflexes and an upgoing left plantar. The right pupil is reactive and 3 mm; visual fields are grossly intact. An urgent non-contrast CT of the brain is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Neurology: Glasgow Coma Scale 14/15 (E4 V4 M6), dysarthria, left hemiparesis (arm 3/5, leg 4/5), left-sided hemisensory loss to pinprick, right-sided cranial nerves intact
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT brain reported normal, blood glucose 5.4 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, no fever, full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg as an adult acute ischaemic stroke pathway now, given the deficit is inside the four and a half hour window
options.rationale: Paediatric acute ischaemic stroke thrombolysis is not routinely offered in Australia and requires confirmed arterial occlusion on MRI/MRA, exclusion of stroke mimics, and specialist involvement. Empirical thrombolysis of a probable hemiplegic migraine attack carries substantial haemorrhage risk without benefit. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)

options.text: Arrange urgent MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging and MRA of the circle of Willis before disease-specific treatment, and consult paediatric neurology now
options.rationale: Non-contrast CT is insensitive for early paediatric ischaemic stroke and cannot exclude arterial dissection or basilar occlusion. Diffusion-weighted MRI with MRA is the definitive investigation, distinguishes hemiplegic migraine (typically normal DWI) from ischaemic stroke (restricted diffusion), and drives all subsequent treatment decisions. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)
source_refs: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus

options.text: Give sumatriptan intranasally at the standard adolescent dose because the family history strongly supports migraine as the underlying diagnosis and defer imaging
options.rationale: Triptans are contraindicated in hemiplegic migraine because of vasoconstrictive potential in the presence of neurological deficit and until stroke is definitively excluded. Family history is supportive but not diagnostic while a fixed hemiparesis is present. (Source: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus)
source_refs: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus

options.text: Start intravenous phenytoin 20 mg/kg loading dose and repeat CT brain in six hours to look for evolving hypodensity before requesting any further imaging
options.rationale: Phenytoin loading is a status epilepticus treatment; there is no witnessed seizure and no evidence of ongoing epileptiform activity. Waiting six hours for CT changes squanders diagnostic time and risks a genuine stroke going untreated. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)

options.text: Start dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus clopidogrel and admit for cardiac echocardiography and full vasculitis workup before advanced imaging
options.rationale: Empirical dual antiplatelet therapy for undifferentiated paediatric neurological deficit is not supported by evidence and carries bleeding risk if imaging reveals intracranial haemorrhage or dissection with an intramural haematoma. Advanced imaging precedes treatment selection. (Source: ANZCS paediatric stroke pathway)

explanation.summary: Hemiplegic migraine is a rare familial migraine subtype defined by aura that includes reversible motor weakness lasting minutes to days, typically alongside visual, sensory or aphasic aura. Paediatric ischaemic stroke is the critical mimic and is missed on non-contrast CT in roughly half of cases at presentation. Diffusion-weighted MRI with MRA is the diagnostic investigation of choice: normal DWI in the presence of hemiparesis strongly supports migraine, while restricted diffusion drives stroke pathways (paediatric-adapted thrombolysis or thrombectomy in select centres). Once stroke and other structural mimics are excluded, hemiplegic migraine attacks are managed with anti-nausea therapy, hydration, analgesia (paracetamol or ibuprofen, avoiding triptans and ergots) and paediatric neurology follow-up for preventive strategy.
key_points: Hemiplegic migraine causes fully reversible motor aura; diagnosis requires exclusion of stroke.
Non-contrast CT is insensitive for paediatric ischaemic stroke; DWI-MRI plus MRA is the investigation of choice.
Triptans and ergots are contraindicated in hemiplegic migraine and while stroke is on the differential.
Familial hemiplegic migraine is autosomal dominant with mutations in CACNA1A, ATP1A2 and SCN1A.
Attack treatment is supportive: hydration, antiemetic, non-triptan analgesia.
explanation.pearls: In a child under 12 with focal neurological deficit and a normal non-contrast CT, arrange MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging within 60 minutes: the absence of restricted diffusion strongly supports hemiplegic migraine over stroke, while its presence opens the paediatric acute stroke pathway.

sources.label: Neurology Society of Australia paediatric migraine consensus

subtopic_detail: Recurrent tracheo-oesophageal fistula versus anastomotic stricture after primary repair
stem:
You are the paediatric surgical registrar reviewing a 6 week old girl who had a primary end-to-end repair of a Gross type C oesophageal atresia with distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula on day one of life. She has a sacral dimple with a tethered cord confirmed on MRI, a horseshoe kidney and a small perimembranous ventricular septal defect. Her right radius is absent.

She was discharged home fully breastfeeding at four weeks after a normal contrast study of the anastomosis. Over the last ten days her mother reports that most feeds now trigger coughing followed by cyanosis, and yesterday she had a witnessed apnoea after a feed. Two episodes of low-grade fever have been attributed to teething. Her weight has fallen from the 25th to the 10th centile.

A chest radiograph today shows a right lower lobe consolidation. A tube oesophagogram performed this morning showed no contrast leak at the anastomosis but a persistent air column tracking anteriorly from the oesophagus toward the trachea above the anastomosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, respiratory rate 62 /min, SpO2 91% on room air rising to 97% on 2 L/min nasal oxygen, temperature 38.1 degC
data_table.Weight: 3.62 kg (fell from 25th to 10th centile in three weeks)
data_table.Examination: Coarse crackles right lower zone, mild subcostal recession, no wheeze, no stridor at rest
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation with no pneumomediastinum; venous blood gas pH 7.36, pCO2 42 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to guide management?

options.text: Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia with methylene blue instilled into the upper oesophageal pouch, in theatre with cardiothoracic and paediatric surgery on standby
options.rationale: The combination of feed-related cyanosis, recurrent right lower lobe pneumonia and a persistent anterior air column above the anastomosis on tube oesophagogram is classic for a recurrent tracheo-oesophageal fistula. Rigid bronchoscopy with methylene blue instilled into the oesophagus and observed on the tracheal side is the reference standard test; it also localises the fistula for the corrective operation. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

options.text: Perform a 24 hour multichannel intraluminal impedance pH study as the initial investigation to quantify acid and non-acid gastro-oesophageal reflux burden
options.rationale: Gastro-oesophageal reflux is common after oesophageal atresia repair and can contribute to aspiration, but MII-pH testing does not detect recurrent fistula and is not the first investigation when the barium study shows a suspicious air column. Reflux workup follows exclusion of a mechanical airway to oesophagus connection. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

options.text: Arrange a fasting hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scintigraphy scan to exclude biliary reflux driven aspiration in a VACTERL infant
options.rationale: HIDA scintigraphy assesses biliary tract patency, not tracheo-oesophageal communication, and has no role in evaluating recurrent aspiration after oesophageal atresia repair. The imaging modalities of value are contrast oesophagogram and rigid bronchoscopy. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

options.text: Request an outpatient videofluoroscopic swallow study by the paediatric speech pathologist as the next investigation before considering repeat surgery
options.rationale: Videofluoroscopy assesses oro-pharyngeal swallow safety; it cannot distinguish aspiration from swallow incoordination from aspiration via a recurrent fistula and delays definitive endoscopic diagnosis in a systemically unwell infant with witnessed apnoea and consolidation. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

options.text: Attempt oesophageal balloon dilatation of a presumed anastomotic stricture under fluoroscopy on the next available list, without endoscopy first
options.rationale: Anastomotic stricture typically presents with progressive dysphagia and food impaction, not feed-triggered cyanosis and pneumonia. Dilating a suspected recurrent fistula site risks converting a small communication into a large one and forces contamination of the mediastinum. Diagnosis precedes intervention. (Source: ANZAPS oesophageal atresia consensus)

explanation.summary: Recurrent tracheo-oesophageal fistula complicates 5-15% of primary oesophageal atresia repairs, usually presenting between four weeks and six months with feed-triggered coughing, cyanotic spells, recurrent right lower lobe aspiration and failure to thrive. The tube oesophagogram may show a linear air column above the anastomosis but is diagnostically insensitive; rigid bronchoscopy with instillation of methylene blue into the oesophagus, watching for dye appearance on the tracheal side, is the reference standard and simultaneously localises the fistula for repair. Alternative diagnoses include anastomotic stricture (progressive dysphagia rather than aspiration), gastro-oesophageal reflux, laryngeal cleft, and vocal cord dysfunction from recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. VACTERL association carries a higher rate of postoperative complications and demands coordinated multidisciplinary follow-up.
key_points: Recurrent TOF classically presents with feed-triggered cyanosis and right lower lobe aspiration.
Tube oesophagogram is insensitive; rigid bronchoscopy with methylene blue is the reference standard.
Anastomotic stricture presents with progressive dysphagia and food bolus impaction, not aspiration.
VACTERL infants require coordinated cardiac, renal, orthopaedic, spinal and airway follow-up.
Repair of recurrent TOF may need pleural or pericardial interposition to prevent second recurrence.
explanation.pearls: In an oesophageal atresia infant with new feed-related cyanosis and right lower lobe pneumonia after day 21, ask theatre for rigid bronchoscopy with methylene blue down the upper pouch: dye on the tracheal side confirms recurrent TOF and localises it for corrective surgery.

subtopic_detail: National cervical screening after LSIL cytology with negative HPV
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 35 year old woman in your clinic. She is asymptomatic, in a stable heterosexual relationship for the last four years, and has three previous normal five-yearly cervical screening tests. She has never had genital warts, no abnormal bleeding, no post-coital bleeding, and no immunosuppression. She has never been pregnant.

Six weeks ago she attended for her routine self-collected cervical screening test as part of a workplace wellbeing programme. The pathology laboratory reports the sample as high-risk human papillomavirus not detected, and a reflex liquid-based cytology performed on the same specimen reports low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) equivalent.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Screening result: HPV oncogenic types 16, 18, and other high-risk types NOT detected; reflex cytology LSIL
data_table.Prior results: Three consecutive negative five-yearly cervical screening tests, last two years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step according to Australia's cervical screening pathway?

options.text: Refer for immediate colposcopy because reflex cytology reports LSIL and any squamous lesion requires visualisation of the transformation zone
options.rationale: Under the primary HPV NCSP algorithm colposcopy is triggered by oncogenic HPV positivity plus a cytology finding, or by HPV 16 or 18 detection regardless of cytology, or by symptomatic bleeding. An LSIL cytology reflex reading with negative high-risk HPV does not itself meet colposcopy criteria in an asymptomatic woman. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Repeat the cervical screening test in twelve months to check for HPV persistence and follow up cytology at the same visit
options.rationale: A 12 month repeat is the algorithm response to a positive HPV result for non-16/18 types with negative or low-grade cytology. It does not apply when the primary HPV test is negative. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Return to routine five-yearly screening because the oncogenic HPV result is negative and there is no cytology-relevant risk without HPV infection
options.rationale: The current NCSP algorithm uses oncogenic HPV as the primary test. When HPV is not detected the risk of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 3 or worse over the next five years is very low, regardless of an incidental cytological finding on the reflex slide. The woman returns to routine five-yearly screening. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Request a repeat clinician-collected liquid-based cytology in eight weeks to confirm the LSIL finding before deciding on further action
options.rationale: Repeat clinician-collected cytology is not indicated when the primary HPV test is negative. Repeating cytology without an HPV trigger reintroduces the pre-2017 pathway that the NCSP moved away from. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange endocervical curettage in the outpatient clinic to exclude a glandular lesion missed on a self-collected sample
options.rationale: Endocervical curettage is a colposcopic procedure reserved for evaluation of possible glandular neoplasia after abnormal HPV or cytology findings. It is not part of the routine screening pathway and is not indicated by an isolated LSIL reading with negative HPV. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Australia's National Cervical Screening Program moved to five-yearly primary HPV testing in December 2017. The screening pathway is driven by the HPV result: HPV not detected returns to five-year recall; HPV 16 or 18 detected goes straight to colposcopy regardless of cytology; other oncogenic HPV detected has reflex cytology, with LSIL or negative cytology triggering a 12 month repeat and HSIL or worse triggering colposcopy. Reflex cytology on an HPV-negative sample is not part of the algorithm and, when it appears (some laboratories report incidental cytology on the primary slide), does not alter management. Symptoms (post-coital bleeding, unexplained inter-menstrual bleeding, persistent discharge) are a separate indication for referral regardless of screening results.
key_points: HPV is the primary test; cytology is reflex only when HPV oncogenic (non-16/18) is detected.
HPV 16 or 18 detected goes straight to colposcopy regardless of cytology.
HPV not detected returns to five-yearly screening irrespective of any incidental cytology finding.
Symptomatic bleeding is a separate colposcopy indication regardless of screening.
Self-collection is now available to all screening-eligible people, not just under-screened groups.
explanation.pearls: In the primary HPV NCSP algorithm an isolated cytology finding on an HPV-negative sample does not change management - the five-year negative predictive value for CIN3 or worse of an HPV-negative sample exceeds 99%.

sources.label: RACGP Red Book preventive health guide

subtopic_detail: Lactational breast abscess management with ongoing breastfeeding
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman four weeks postpartum. She has been exclusively breastfeeding her first baby who is thriving on the 50th centile. Three days ago she felt a hard painful red patch in her left upper outer quadrant and was started on oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times a day and warm compresses by an out-of-hours doctor.

Despite good adherence, her fever has continued and the area has now formed a distinct rounded lump that is tender and fluctuant. She has not had chills for the last six hours. She is otherwise well, without cellulitis beyond the affected quadrant, no nipple crack and no rash. She is very keen to continue breastfeeding and is still latching the baby to the affected breast, which is painful but tolerated.

Bedside ultrasound performed in your clinic shows a 3.5 cm x 2.8 cm hypoechoic collection with internal echoes at 3 cm depth, with no involvement of the areola.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.3 degC
data_table.Examination: Erythema and induration left upper outer quadrant, discrete 3.5 cm fluctuant lump, no cellulitis beyond quadrant, no lymphangitis, no crack in the nipple
data_table.Investigations: Bedside breast ultrasound: 3.5 cm x 2.8 cm hypoechoic collection with internal echoes at 3 cm depth, no involvement of the areola

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue oral flucloxacillin at the same dose and add oral metronidazole for anaerobic cover, reviewing her in clinic at 72 hours before considering drainage
options.rationale: A drainable collection larger than 3 cm will not resolve with oral antibiotics alone. Delayed drainage risks sinus formation, further breast tissue destruction and possible skin ulceration. Antibiotic modification without drainage is insufficient once fluctuance and imaging confirm an abscess. (Source: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update)
source_refs: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update

options.text: Perform ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle aspiration under local anaesthesia, send pus for culture, continue oral flucloxacillin and support ongoing breastfeeding
options.rationale: Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is the first-line drainage for a lactational breast abscess under about 5 cm without skin necrosis. It preserves cosmesis, permits ongoing breastfeeding, and carries lower recurrence than incision. Antibiotics remain because the surrounding tissue is still cellulitic. Culture guides ongoing therapy. (Source: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update)
source_refs: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update
eTG Complete Antibiotic: mastitis and breast abscess

options.text: Arrange emergency incision and drainage in theatre under general anaesthesia and advise the mother to formula-feed the baby until the surgical wound has fully healed
options.rationale: Formal incision and drainage under general anaesthesia is reserved for large abscesses over 5 cm, abscesses with skin necrosis, or those that fail image-guided aspiration. Cessation of breastfeeding increases the risk of milk stasis and recurrence and is not required for either drainage approach. (Source: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update)
source_refs: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update

options.text: Advise complete cessation of breastfeeding on the affected side, prescribe cabergoline to suppress milk supply, and continue oral flucloxacillin without drainage
options.rationale: Cabergoline suppression is contraindicated by the patient's clear preference to continue breastfeeding and is medically unnecessary. Ongoing milk removal from the affected breast (feeding, hand expression) accelerates resolution. The abscess still requires drainage. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: mastitis and breast abscess)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: mastitis and breast abscess

options.text: Refer for urgent core biopsy of the mass to exclude inflammatory breast carcinoma before proceeding to any percutaneous or surgical drainage of the lesion
options.rationale: Inflammatory breast carcinoma is a red-flag differential in non-lactating women with erythema and peau d'orange, or when a suspected abscess does not resolve after adequate drainage and antibiotics. It is not the first-line workup for a fluctuant lump with a clear ultrasound abscess appearance in the fourth postpartum week. (Source: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update)
source_refs: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis affects around 15% of breastfeeding women in the first six weeks. Most cases respond to milk removal, warm compresses and oral flucloxacillin, but a proportion progress to abscess formation and require drainage. Bedside ultrasound is diagnostic and quantifies size. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle aspiration is first-line for abscesses under about 5 cm without skin necrosis; it preserves cosmesis, allows continued breastfeeding, and has an aspiration-to-cure rate over 80% with repeat aspirations as needed. Larger abscesses, skin necrosis, or aspiration failure escalate to formal incision and drainage. Breastfeeding from the affected breast should continue where tolerated, as milk stasis worsens outcomes and expressed milk supports supply.
key_points: Mastitis unresponsive to 48-72 hours of antibiotics and milk removal warrants ultrasound to look for abscess.
Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration is first line for lactational abscess under 5 cm without skin necrosis.
Continue breastfeeding from the affected breast; formula-only is not indicated.
Repeat aspirations may be needed every 2-3 days until pus has resolved.
Non-resolving mass after adequate drainage and antibiotics: consider inflammatory breast cancer and refer for imaging plus biopsy.
explanation.pearls: A hypoechoic collection over 3 cm with internal echoes on bedside ultrasound is a lactational abscess until proven otherwise - continue flucloxacillin, aspirate under ultrasound guidance, and keep the mother breastfeeding on the affected side.

sources.label: RACGP AJGP lactational breast abscess update
eTG Complete Antibiotic: mastitis and breast abscess

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for Group B streptococcus with previous affected sibling
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman at 36 plus 3 weeks in the antenatal clinic. Her first baby, now three years old, had culture-confirmed Group B streptococcal early-onset sepsis at 20 hours of life and made a full recovery after IV benzylpenicillin. In her current pregnancy the routine 36 week rectovaginal screening swab reports Group B streptococcus not detected.

She has no known drug allergies, no significant medical history, and no prior preterm birth. Her BMI is 24 kg/m^2. She is planning a vaginal birth in a public tertiary hospital with continuous CTG monitoring available.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Antenatal screening: 36-week rectovaginal Group B streptococcus swab: NOT detected; urine culture from booking negative
data_table.Obstetric history: First baby with culture-confirmed early-onset GBS sepsis at 20 hours; treated to recovery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic plan?

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g every four hours until birth, commenced in labour or at membrane rupture whichever is earlier during this admission
options.rationale: Previous infant with invasive GBS disease is a RANZCOG standalone indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis irrespective of current screening. First-line agent is IV benzylpenicillin with a 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g four-hourly, starting in established labour or at membrane rupture, and continuing until birth. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

options.text: No intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is required because the current 36-week rectovaginal swab is negative and screening supersedes prior obstetric history
options.rationale: A previous infant with invasive GBS disease is a standalone indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis regardless of the current pregnancy's screening result. The vertical transmission risk is judged too high to rely on culture alone. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times a day from 37 weeks continued until the onset of labour to eradicate any low-level Group B streptococcal genital colonisation
options.rationale: Antenatal oral antibiotics do not durably eradicate GBS colonisation and are not part of the Australian prophylaxis pathway. Intrapartum intravenous prophylaxis is what reduces vertical transmission and early-onset disease. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

options.text: IV vancomycin 20 mg/kg every eight hours from admission in labour, given the severity of the Group B streptococcal disease that occurred in her previous baby
options.rationale: Vancomycin is reserved for women with a documented immediate hypersensitivity to penicillin AND either clindamycin resistance on GBS isolate or clindamycin susceptibility unknown. Severity of prior disease does not change the first-line agent. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

options.text: Recommend elective caesarean at 39 weeks to bypass the birth canal and avoid the need for any intrapartum intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis during her labour
options.rationale: A prior baby with GBS sepsis is not itself an indication for caesarean. Elective caesarean on intact membranes before labour eliminates the immediate intrapartum transmission risk but does not obviate GBS prophylaxis in women with strong risk factors, and adds surgical morbidity. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

explanation.summary: Group B streptococcus colonises the maternal genital tract in around 20% of Australian women and is the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis. RANZCOG endorses a risk-and-screening hybrid: 35-37 week rectovaginal swab identifies most carriers, with intrapartum IV benzylpenicillin offered to carriers, women with GBS bacteriuria in this pregnancy, women with a previous baby who had invasive GBS disease, and unbooked women in preterm labour or with prolonged rupture of membranes over 18 hours or intrapartum fever above 38 degrees regardless of screening. Effective prophylaxis requires the first dose at least four hours before birth. Alternative agents are chosen by penicillin allergy severity and antibiogram.
key_points: Previous baby with invasive GBS disease = standalone indication for IAP regardless of current swab.
First-line IAP: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g four-hourly until birth.
Effective prophylaxis requires at least four hours between first dose and delivery.
Penicillin non-severe hypersensitivity: cefazolin 2 g load then 1 g every 8 hours.
Penicillin severe hypersensitivity: clindamycin if isolate susceptible, otherwise IV vancomycin.
explanation.pearls: A prior baby with invasive GBS disease overrides a negative current-pregnancy swab: give IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every four hours from established labour or rupture of membranes, aiming for at least four hours before birth.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus

subtopic_detail: Investigation pathway after three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman in the outpatient clinic. She and her partner have had three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages over the last two years at 8, 6 and 9 weeks; all were confirmed with a positive urine pregnancy test and each was managed expectantly with confirmed complete miscarriage on transvaginal ultrasound.

She has regular 28 day menstrual cycles and no history of pelvic inflammatory disease. Her BMI is 26 kg/m^2, she does not smoke or drink alcohol and takes no medications. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. Her partner is fit and well.

She saw a naturopath privately and had a karyotype on the tissue from the most recent loss which reports a euploid 46 XY specimen.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Non-tender abdomen; normal external genitalia; uterus anteverted and mobile on bimanual
data_table.Prior investigations: Product of conception karyotype from third loss: 46 XY euploid

lead_in: Which set of investigations is most appropriate as first-line workup?

options.text: Sperm DNA fragmentation testing and detailed semen analysis as first-line, deferring maternal blood work until the paternal contribution has been clarified
options.rationale: Sperm DNA fragmentation testing is not routinely recommended in recurrent pregnancy loss workup and has an uncertain evidence base for changing management. Maternal-side treatable causes take priority. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Inherited thrombophilia panel including factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene mutation, protein C and S, antithrombin, homocysteine and MTHFR polymorphism screen only
options.rationale: Routine inherited thrombophilia screening is NOT recommended in recurrent miscarriage: results do not alter management, MTHFR is now specifically discouraged, and false positives lead to unnecessary anticoagulation exposure. Reserve for a personal or family VTE history. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: TORCH serology, cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM, herpes simplex virus 1 and 2, and toxoplasma IgG and IgM as the initial workup before any structural investigation
options.rationale: TORCH infections are not causes of recurrent first-trimester miscarriage. Screening produces prevalence findings without therapeutic implications and delays workup of the causes that do matter. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Endometrial biopsy for chronic endometritis with bacterial and mycoplasma culture and empirical treatment with a two-week course of doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
options.rationale: The evidence for chronic endometritis as a cause of recurrent pregnancy loss and for empirical doxycycline is limited and this is not a RANZCOG first-line investigation. Consider only in the context of investigation-negative recurrent loss with tertiary specialist input. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Antiphospholipid antibody screen on two occasions twelve weeks apart, thyroid function, parental karyotypes, and pelvic imaging with three-dimensional ultrasound or hysterosalpingography
options.rationale: RANZCOG and ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guidelines identify treatable causes: antiphospholipid syndrome (needs two positive tests 12 weeks apart), thyroid dysfunction, parental balanced translocations and uterine cavity anomalies. This is the evidence-based first-line panel that changes management. (Source: RANZCOG C-Gyn 40 Recurrent miscarriage)

explanation.summary: Recurrent pregnancy loss is defined by RANZCOG as three or more consecutive first-trimester miscarriages. The evidence-based workup targets treatable or prognostically important conditions: antiphospholipid syndrome (repeat testing 12 weeks apart to satisfy classification criteria), thyroid dysfunction, parental balanced chromosomal translocations, and uterine cavity anomalies (septum, submucosal fibroid, adhesions). Approximately half of couples end investigation with no identified cause; supportive care with early-pregnancy ultrasound in the next conception is offered and cumulative live-birth rates remain reasonable. Empirical progesterone (400 mg vaginally twice daily) started with a positive test may be offered per the RANZCOG algorithm to women with a history of recurrent miscarriage and early pregnancy bleeding.
key_points: Recurrent miscarriage per RANZCOG: three or more consecutive first-trimester losses.
First-line workup: APLS (twice, 12 weeks apart), TFTs, parental karyotype, uterine cavity imaging.
Routine inherited thrombophilia and MTHFR screening are NOT recommended.
Empirical vaginal progesterone can be offered when bleeding occurs in the next pregnancy.
About 50% remain unexplained; supportive care and early scan the primary intervention.
explanation.pearls: Do NOT order MTHFR or routine thrombophilia in recurrent miscarriage - the evidence supports lupus anticoagulant plus anticardiolipin plus anti-beta-2 glycoprotein-I repeated at 12 weeks, thyroid function, parental karyotypes, and uterine cavity imaging.

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia detected at second trimester scan
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 33 year old primigravida in the maternal-foetal medicine clinic at 32 plus 4 weeks. Her pregnancy was conceived by fresh embryo transfer following IVF and has been otherwise uncomplicated with a normal foetal anomaly scan.

A tertiary transvaginal ultrasound with colour Doppler was arranged after the 20 week anomaly scan reported a low-lying velamentous cord insertion. Today's scan confirms a velamentous cord insertion in the lower posterior segment with a foetal vessel running unprotected across the internal os on colour Doppler. The placenta is otherwise 3.6 cm from the internal os and there is no morbidly adherent appearance.

She has no bleeding, no contractions and no rupture of membranes. Booking bloods and glucose tolerance test are normal. Foetal growth is on the 55th centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler and reactive cardiotocograph. She lives 45 minutes from the tertiary hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits, foetal heart rate 138 /min
data_table.Ultrasound: Velamentous cord insertion, foetal vessel over internal os (vasa praevia); placental edge 3.6 cm from os; EFW 55th centile; UA Doppler normal; AFI 14 cm
data_table.CTG: Baseline 140, variability 10, accelerations present, no decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Admit at 32 weeks for inpatient monitoring with a completed course of antenatal corticosteroids, aim for planned caesarean between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks
options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends inpatient admission for confirmed vasa praevia from around 30-32 weeks with a completed corticosteroid course, given the risk of catastrophic foetal haemorrhage at rupture of membranes. Planned caesarean between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks balances perinatal exsanguination risk against prematurity. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Continue outpatient antenatal follow-up with weekly CTG from 36 weeks, aim for spontaneous labour and vaginal birth at term with continuous intrapartum monitoring
options.rationale: Vaginal birth in vasa praevia carries a perinatal mortality above 50% because rupture of the foetal vessel at membrane rupture leads to rapid foetal exsanguination. Planned caesarean before labour is the standard of care. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Arrange an emergency cervical cerclage at 33 weeks to reinforce the lower uterine segment, and plan spontaneous vaginal birth at term
options.rationale: Cerclage does not treat vasa praevia and is not indicated. The condition is a foetal vessel problem, not a cervical competency problem. Vaginal birth remains contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Arrange induction of labour at 37 weeks with amniotomy avoided until the presenting part is well applied, and immediate caesarean for any bleeding
options.rationale: Attempted vaginal birth places the foetus at unacceptable risk of exsanguination at any spontaneous or artificial membrane rupture. Induction of labour does not mitigate this risk and is contrary to RANZCOG guidance. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean at 39 weeks after a second course of corticosteroids at 38 weeks to minimise iatrogenic prematurity
options.rationale: Delaying planned caesarean to 39 weeks in vasa praevia substantially increases the probability of spontaneous labour or rupture of membranes with catastrophic foetal haemorrhage. RANZCOG recommends birth by 35+6 weeks. Two courses of corticosteroids beyond 34 weeks are not routine. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 47 Vasa praevia)

explanation.summary: Vasa praevia is unprotected foetal vessels crossing the internal cervical os, either from a velamentous cord insertion (type I) or between placental lobes in a bilobed or succenturiate placenta (type II). Antenatal diagnosis by second-trimester ultrasound with follow-up transvaginal colour Doppler transforms outcomes: undiagnosed vasa praevia carries a perinatal mortality above 50%, diagnosed cases with planned caesarean carry a survival rate approaching 100%. RANZCOG advises inpatient admission from 30-32 weeks (individualised for distance from hospital and clinical stability), a completed corticosteroid course, and planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks. Emergency caesarean with massive transfusion capability follows any antepartum haemorrhage, ruptured membranes or spontaneous labour.
key_points: Vasa praevia carries perinatal mortality above 50% when undiagnosed; near 100% survival with planned birth.
Type I: velamentous cord insertion. Type II: vessels between lobes.
Admit from 30-32 weeks; complete antenatal corticosteroids by 34 weeks.
Planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks (SMFM 34-37, RANZCOG typically 34-36).
Emergency caesarean for any bleeding, rupture of membranes, or labour.
explanation.pearls: In a confirmed vasa praevia, plan the caesarean between 34+0 and 35+6 weeks after an antenatal corticosteroid course and admit the mother from around 32 weeks - waiting until 39 weeks converts a survivable situation into a foetal exsanguination emergency.

subtopic_detail: Post-caesarean pharmacological VTE prophylaxis in obesity
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman on the postnatal ward six hours after an emergency in-labour caesarean for foetal distress. She is her second baby. Her BMI at booking was 41 kg/m^2 and her measured weight today is 118 kg. She had gestational diabetes managed with insulin.

She had a category 2 caesarean at 39 plus 2 weeks under spinal anaesthesia; the estimated blood loss was 900 mL and the wound was closed with staples. She lost 1300 mL total by 4 hours postpartum but her haemodynamics and urine output are now stable, she is not bleeding actively per vaginam, and the postnatal haemoglobin is 105 g/L.

She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism, no known thrombophilia, and no current epidural in situ. She is exclusively breastfeeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Postnatal bloods: Haemoglobin 105 g/L (115-165), platelets 244 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), INR 1.0
data_table.Anticoagulant history: No anticoagulation antepartum; last thromboprophylaxis assessment antenatally scored as intermediate risk

lead_in: What is the most appropriate pharmacological thromboprophylaxis plan?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg orally daily for six weeks as VTE prophylaxis rather than low molecular weight heparin because of the risk of postpartum haemorrhage after this caesarean
options.rationale: Aspirin is not an accepted postpartum VTE prophylactic agent under RANZCOG or RCOG guidance. Low molecular weight heparin at a weight-adjusted dose is standard for postpartum women meeting risk thresholds, once haemostasis is secured. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

options.text: Oral rivaroxaban 10 mg daily for six weeks postpartum, with a switch to warfarin only if her breastfeeding continues beyond that time and further prophylaxis is needed
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants including rivaroxaban are not recommended in breastfeeding women because transfer into breast milk is either significant or inadequately characterised. LMWH is breastfeeding-compatible. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

options.text: Standard-dose enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for ten days from the day after her surgery, with graduated compression stockings continued for the full six weeks
options.rationale: The RANZCOG weight-adjustment schedule delivers approximately 0.6 mg/kg for extended prophylaxis; 40 mg is under-dosing for 118 kg. Ten days does not meet the guideline recommendation of six weeks postpartum LMWH for women with multiple moderate risk factors. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

options.text: Therapeutic-dose enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice a day for six weeks postpartum given her obesity, gestational diabetes and category 2 caesarean earlier today
options.rationale: Therapeutic dose LMWH is reserved for confirmed or high-clinical-suspicion VTE, mechanical valve prophylaxis, or specific antiphospholipid syndrome scenarios. It carries substantial bleeding risk and is not indicated for postpartum prophylaxis in the absence of documented VTE. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

options.text: Weight-adjusted enoxaparin 80 mg subcutaneously daily for six weeks, commencing at least four hours after any neuraxial catheter is removed and haemostasis is secured
options.rationale: Emergency in-labour caesarean plus BMI over 40 plus current weight over 90 kg constitutes multiple moderate-risk factors, meeting the RANZCOG threshold for six weeks postpartum LMWH. Weight-based dosing per RANZCOG is 0.6 mg/kg once daily rounded to available vial size for weights 91-130 kg, approximating enoxaparin 80 mg. Timing after neuraxial anaesthesia respects catheter removal rules. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 29 VTE and pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Pregnancy and the puerperium raise VTE risk fourfold antenatally and up to twentyfold postnatally, with the peak in the first six weeks post-delivery. RANZCOG stratifies risk by antenatal and postnatal factors: BMI at booking above 30, emergency caesarean, prolonged labour, immobility, peripartum haemorrhage requiring transfusion, pre-eclampsia, prior VTE and known thrombophilia. Women with multiple moderate risk factors after caesarean receive weight-adjusted enoxaparin for six weeks postpartum; LMWH is preferred over unfractionated heparin except in renal failure. Neuraxial block timing rules apply: first prophylactic LMWH dose is given at least four hours after removal of an epidural catheter and prophylactic dosing precedes any subsequent catheter removal by at least 12 hours.
key_points: Multiple moderate risk factors (emergency CS + BMI > 40 + weight > 90 kg) meet RANZCOG threshold for 6 week postpartum LMWH.
Weight-adjusted enoxaparin approximates 0.6 mg/kg daily; 91-130 kg dose is around 80 mg daily.
Aspirin is NOT an accepted postpartum VTE prophylactic agent.
DOACs are not recommended while breastfeeding; LMWH and warfarin are compatible.
Timing after neuraxial block: at least 4 hours after catheter removal for LMWH.
explanation.pearls: For postpartum VTE prophylaxis at booking BMI over 40, use enoxaparin 0.6 mg/kg daily (about 80 mg for 118 kg) for six weeks - the risk peak is in the first six weeks post-delivery, and shorter courses miss the majority of pulmonary emboli.

subtopic_detail: Suspected placenta accreta spectrum after two prior caesareans
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 36 year old woman at 28 plus 3 weeks in a metropolitan tertiary hospital antenatal clinic. She has had two previous lower segment caesarean sections. The current pregnancy was conceived spontaneously and is her third; her second baby was born 18 months ago.

Today's ultrasound reports an anterior placenta covering the internal os with multiple placental lacunae, loss of the retroplacental clear space, focal thinning of the myometrium to 1 mm behind the placenta with bridging vessels between the placenta and the bladder wall on colour Doppler. Foetal growth is on the 60th centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler.

She has no bleeding, no contractions, and no rupture of membranes. Her booking bloods and gestational diabetes screen were normal. She lives 20 minutes from the tertiary centre.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits, foetal heart rate 142 /min
data_table.Ultrasound: Anterior placenta covering internal os; multiple placental lacunae (Finberg grade 3); loss of retroplacental clear space; myometrium 1 mm; bladder wall bridging vessels
data_table.Booking bloods: Haemoglobin 122 g/L (115-165), platelets 235 x10^9/L (150-400), ABO A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Continue outpatient antenatal care with a repeat ultrasound at 34 weeks and aim for elective caesarean at 38 plus 6 weeks in a suitably resourced tertiary hospital
options.rationale: Delaying elective caesarean to 39 weeks in suspected placenta accreta spectrum substantially increases the probability of an emergency haemorrhage. RANZCOG and international guidance both recommend planned birth between 34 and 36 weeks after a completed corticosteroid course. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.text: Confirm ultrasound with MRI placenta, complete antenatal corticosteroids at 34 weeks, and plan a multidisciplinary caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in an accreta centre
options.rationale: Placenta praevia with two prior caesareans plus lacunae, loss of clear space, bridging vessels and myometrial thinning meets the ultrasound criteria for likely placenta accreta spectrum. MRI adds surgical planning information. Planned birth at 34+0-35+6 weeks in a placenta accreta centre with multidisciplinary team, blood bank preparation and planned caesarean hysterectomy is standard of care. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.text: Arrange bilateral uterine artery embolisation under interventional radiology now and plan vaginal birth after two caesareans at 37 weeks with placenta left in situ post-birth
options.rationale: Vaginal birth is contraindicated with placenta praevia. Prophylactic pre-birth embolisation is not standard practice for antenatally suspected accreta spectrum in Australia; balloon catheters may have a role intraoperatively at select centres, not as an outpatient antenatal intervention. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.text: Admit at 30 weeks for weekly transvaginal cervical length and daily cardiotocography, aiming for spontaneous labour and vaginal birth at term with continuous fetal monitoring
options.rationale: Vaginal birth is contraindicated with placenta praevia and additionally with suspected accreta. Cervical length screening does not alter management here and daily CTG antenatally in an otherwise stable pregnancy adds no value. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

options.text: Arrange emergency caesarean today under general anaesthesia with immediate abdominal hysterectomy, given the very high risk of catastrophic obstetric haemorrhage at 28 weeks
options.rationale: Emergency delivery at 28 weeks in a stable woman inflicts substantial prematurity morbidity unnecessarily. Planned delivery at 34+0-35+6 weeks after corticosteroids in a suitably resourced centre is the standard, with emergency intervention reserved for antepartum haemorrhage or labour. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta

explanation.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum is defined by abnormal placental adherence (accreta), invasion into myometrium (increta) or through it (percreta). Prior caesarean plus a current anterior placenta praevia is the leading risk profile; two prior caesareans raises accreta risk to around 40%. Antenatal ultrasound features include placental lacunae (Finberg grade), loss of the retroplacental clear space, myometrial thinning, bladder wall interruption and bridging vessels. MRI is not diagnostic in isolation but adds surgical planning value. Standard care is planned caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a placenta accreta centre with obstetrics, gynaecological oncology or urology, anaesthesia, interventional radiology, blood bank and neonatal intensive care coordinated. Caesarean hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ is the usual surgical strategy; conservative management with the placenta left in situ and expectant care is offered in select cases.
key_points: Two prior caesareans plus anterior praevia carries around 40% accreta risk.
Key ultrasound features: lacunae (grade 3), loss of clear space, myometrial thinning, bridging vessels.
MRI supports surgical planning, not diagnosis in isolation.
Planned caesarean at 34+0-35+6 weeks after corticosteroids in an accreta centre.
Standard strategy is caesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ.
explanation.pearls: In a woman with two prior caesareans and an anterior placenta praevia showing lacunae, loss of the clear space, and bridging vessels at 28 weeks, the correct sequence is MRI plus corticosteroids plus transfer to a placenta accreta centre for planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0-35+6 weeks.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 20 Placenta praevia and accreta
