subtopic_detail: Retained placenta with concurrent atony despite pharmacological uterotonics
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to a delivery suite room 40 minutes after the vaginal birth of a term baby to a 31 year old woman on her third pregnancy. She has had two prior spontaneous vaginal births without complication. The placenta has not delivered despite active management with IM oxytocin 10 units, controlled cord traction and maternal effort.

The midwife reports 900 mL of estimated ongoing PV loss over the last 15 minutes with a boggy uterus that briefly firms with fundal massage then relaxes. A second dose of intramuscular oxytocin has been given and an IV infusion of oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's is running at 250 mL/h. The umbilical cord is intact and the placenta is felt as a discrete mass in the mid-uterine cavity on abdominal palpation.

She is pale, cool peripherally, with fingertip capillary refill three seconds and no epidural in situ. Two 16 gauge IV cannulae have been sited; four units of cross-matched red cells are already in the room.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 84/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 degC
data_table.Estimated blood loss: 1600 mL total; 900 mL in last 15 minutes; ongoing
data_table.Bedside: Bladder scanner 40 mL, uterus boggy at umbilicus firms briefly to fundal massage, cord intact, placenta palpable in mid-cavity, no visible cervical or vaginal tear
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care haemoglobin 78 g/L (115-165); coagulation not yet available; fibrinogen not yet available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a further 250 microgram intramuscular ergometrine, insert a Bakri intrauterine balloon, and reassess her response to combined pharmacological therapy over the next 30 minutes
options.rationale: A Bakri balloon has no role while the placenta remains in the uterus; the tamponade cannot form around a foreign body of that size. Continued pharmacological uterotonics without addressing the retained placenta will not stop the bleeding and delays definitive treatment. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol, transfer to theatre for manual removal of the placenta under anaesthesia with concurrent intravenous tranexamic acid and antibiotics
options.rationale: The woman is haemodynamically unstable with a retained placenta and atonic haemorrhage. Manual removal under anaesthesia is the definitive treatment; delay adds ongoing exsanguination. Simultaneous massive transfusion activation, IV tranexamic acid within three hours of birth (WOMAN trial) and prophylactic antibiotics (single-dose cefazolin plus metronidazole) form the standard package. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.text: Attempt umbilical vein injection of 30 units of oxytocin diluted in 30 mL of normal saline via a catheter to encourage placental separation before considering manual removal
options.rationale: Umbilical vein oxytocin has weak evidence of benefit for retained placenta and no role in an unstable haemorrhaging woman. The definitive treatment remains theatre transfer for manual removal. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.text: Perform bedside manual removal of the placenta in the delivery room using nitrous oxide analgesia only, and transfuse packed red cells to her as soon as they become available
options.rationale: Bedside manual removal without adequate anaesthesia is painful, unsafe, and produces incomplete removal; it also delays the surgical response if bleeding does not settle. RANZCOG mandates regional or general anaesthesia in an appropriately equipped theatre. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

options.text: Arrange interventional radiology for uterine artery embolisation before surgical intervention, with vasopressor support to maintain her blood pressure in the meantime here
options.rationale: Interventional radiology is not the first-line response to retained placenta with ongoing haemorrhage. The retained placenta must be removed; embolisation is considered after removal if atony or focal bleeding persists. Vasopressor use without volume resuscitation and definitive haemostasis worsens end-organ perfusion. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

explanation.summary: Retained placenta is defined by RANZCOG as failure of placental delivery beyond 30 minutes of active third-stage management. In an actively bleeding woman it converts a common third-stage problem into an obstetric emergency, because the partially-separated placenta prevents effective uterine contraction and creates open sinuses at the placental bed. Definitive treatment is manual removal under regional or general anaesthesia. The standard concurrent package is massive transfusion protocol activation for major PPH, tranexamic acid 1 g IV within three hours of birth (WOMAN trial shows a mortality benefit), and single-dose prophylactic antibiotics (cefazolin plus metronidazole). Ongoing atony after removal escalates through uterotonic ladder, uterine balloon tamponade, uterine compression sutures, uterine artery embolisation, and finally hysterectomy.
key_points: Retained placenta: no delivery of placenta within 30 minutes of active third-stage management.
In a bleeding woman, retained placenta prevents uterine contraction; manual removal is the definitive treatment.
Give IV tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours of birth for any PPH (WOMAN trial mortality benefit).
Uterine balloon tamponade requires an empty uterus, not one containing a retained placenta.
Post-removal atony ladder: oxytocin infusion -> ergometrine -> carboprost -> tamponade -> compression sutures -> embolisation -> hysterectomy.
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV within three hours of birth reduces death from bleeding by around a third in the WOMAN trial; the retained placenta must be removed in theatre first, because uterine balloon tamponade cannot form around a placenta.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention and management of PPH

subtopic_detail: Smoking cessation pharmacotherapy in a patient stabilised on clozapine
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 47 year old man in the community mental health team clinic. He has schizophrenia stable on clozapine 400 mg nightly for the last five years without hospitalisation. His last clozapine plasma level was 480 microg/L six weeks ago (target 350-600 for optimal response).

He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 30 years and now wants to quit. He has no history of seizures, no current depressive episode, and no recent suicidal ideation. His BMI is 32 kg/m^2 with hypertension controlled on ramipril. Renal function and liver function are within normal limits. He has an active e-cigarette prescription he says he does not use.

He asks about pharmacological help to stop smoking and specifically wants to know if the tablet he read about is safe with his mental health medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 400 mg nightly (level 480 microg/L six weeks ago), ramipril 5 mg daily
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), ALT 28 U/L (<40)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy plan?

options.text: Start nortriptyline 25 mg at night up-titrated to 75 mg at night as a smoking cessation adjunct and continue his clozapine 400 mg nightly at the same dose throughout the quit attempt
options.rationale: Nortriptyline is second-line for smoking cessation and is not first-line in Australia. Adding a sedating tricyclic to clozapine adds anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension risk, and QT prolongation, none of which are needed given first-line agents are available. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

options.text: Start bupropion 150 mg daily for three days then 150 mg twice daily for twelve weeks and continue clozapine unchanged at his current 400 mg nightly dose during his quit attempt
options.rationale: Bupropion lowers seizure threshold, an already relevant risk on clozapine (which reduces seizure threshold in a dose-dependent way), and is a poor first-line choice in this specific patient. Failing to anticipate the CYP1A2 de-induction effect on clozapine levels risks toxicity. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: clozapine)

options.text: Start varenicline 0.5 mg daily for three days then 0.5 mg twice daily for four days then 1 mg twice daily for twelve weeks, monitor clozapine levels, and consider a 25% clozapine dose reduction at quit date
options.rationale: Varenicline is the most effective monotherapy for smoking cessation. Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A2 and increases clozapine clearance; cessation causes clozapine levels to rise by roughly 50%, risking toxicity, so a dose reduction of about 25% at the quit date with plasma level monitoring is standard. Varenicline itself is not contraindicated in stable schizophrenia. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: clozapine)

options.text: Prescribe combination nicotine replacement using a 21 mg 24-hour patch plus lozenges for cravings only, and continue clozapine unchanged at his current 400 mg nightly dose
options.rationale: Combination NRT is a reasonable second-line, but it does not remove the need to anticipate rising clozapine levels once he actually stops smoking (nicotine itself does not induce CYP1A2 - the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in smoke do). Failing to reduce clozapine at quit day risks toxicity. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: clozapine)

options.text: Advise abrupt cessation using willpower alone and refer to a peer-support smoking cessation programme; avoid all pharmacotherapy given that he takes clozapine 400 mg nightly for schizophrenia
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation without pharmacotherapy has the lowest quit rate at 12 months. Refusing pharmacotherapy in patients with severe mental illness is contrary to the RACGP smoking cessation guideline. Clozapine is not itself a contraindication to any Australian first-line smoking cessation drug. (Source: RACGP Supporting smoking cessation)

explanation.summary: Smoking rates among people with schizophrenia are two to three times the general population and drive much of the mortality gap. First-line smoking cessation pharmacotherapies in Australia are varenicline (most effective monotherapy), combination NRT (patch plus fast-acting), and bupropion. Bupropion is avoided when seizure risk is heightened, including on clozapine. Varenicline was previously flagged for neuropsychiatric concerns; the EAGLES trial found no increased risk in stable severe mental illness, and it is now used routinely in this group. Critically, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke induce CYP1A2, the primary metaboliser of clozapine and olanzapine; smoking cessation de-induces CYP1A2 over 1-4 weeks, raising clozapine levels by around 50% and risking toxicity (sedation, hypersalivation, seizures, myocarditis). A pre-emptive 25% clozapine dose reduction at the quit date with plasma level monitoring is standard.
key_points: Varenicline is first-line monotherapy; EAGLES trial supports safety in stable severe mental illness.
Bupropion lowers seizure threshold; a poor choice alongside clozapine.
Tobacco smoke (not nicotine) induces CYP1A2; smoking cessation raises clozapine levels ~50%.
Reduce clozapine dose by about 25% at quit date and monitor plasma levels.
Combination NRT (patch plus lozenge/gum) is more effective than either alone.
explanation.pearls: When a smoker on clozapine stops smoking, expect the plasma level to rise about 50% over one to four weeks - drop the clozapine dose by around 25% on quit day and repeat the level at two and four weeks.

subtopic_detail: Adult ADHD diagnosis and stimulant initiation in the context of anxiety and driving
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28 year old software developer at outpatient clinic. He was referred by his general practitioner with lifelong difficulty sustaining attention, disorganisation and frequent lateness that have worsened since he started a full-time job two years ago. He describes restless-inside feelings, jumping between tabs constantly, and reading the same email paragraph six times.

His school reports from age 8 documented forgetfulness, avoidance of homework, and inattentive behaviour in class. He drives a car about 200 km per week to visit his parents. He drinks less than five standard drinks a week, does not use methamphetamine or cocaine, and has no history of psychosis or bipolar disorder.

You elicit a DIVA-5 structured assessment consistent with combined-presentation ADHD in childhood and persisting into adulthood, plus concurrent generalised anxiety disorder (GAD-7 score 12) which pre-dates the ADHD symptoms getting worse. Blood pressure is 118/74, ECG shows sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Screening scores: ASRS positive; DIVA-5 meets combined presentation ADHD; GAD-7 12/21 (moderate)
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm at 72 /min with QTc 410 ms and no ischaemic changes; thyroid function within normal limits; urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment plan?

options.text: Start atomoxetine 40 mg daily up-titrating to 80 mg after two weeks and avoid all stimulants because his comorbid anxiety and long-distance driving history make stimulants inappropriate now
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second-line unless stimulants are contraindicated. Anxiety and long-distance driving are not stimulant contraindications; treated ADHD improves rather than worsens driving safety and stimulant-related anxiety worsening is often manageable with dose titration. (Source: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based)
source_refs: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based

options.text: Start immediate release methylphenidate 5 mg twice daily up-titrating fortnightly to therapeutic effect, alongside a course of cognitive behavioural therapy for his moderate generalised anxiety
options.rationale: Australian ADHD guidelines recommend a stimulant as first-line for adult ADHD without a contraindication (uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmia, active substance use disorder). Methylphenidate at low dose with fortnightly titration allows monitoring of anxiety, cardiovascular and sleep effects. Concurrent CBT addresses the GAD without a benzodiazepine. (Source: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based)
source_refs: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based

options.text: Prescribe diazepam 5 mg twice daily to manage his anxiety symptoms first and defer any ADHD-specific pharmacological treatment until his generalised anxiety disorder is fully controlled
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not first-line for GAD, carry dependence and cognitive impairment risks, and worsen inattention. Deferring ADHD treatment indefinitely while adding a benzodiazepine is harmful. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: anxiety disorders)

options.text: Start bupropion 150 mg extended release daily up-titrating to 300 mg per day as an off-label agent covering both his ADHD symptoms and his moderate generalised anxiety symptoms concurrently
options.rationale: Bupropion has some off-label evidence in adult ADHD but is not a first-line agent under Australian guidance and its noradrenergic activity typically worsens anxiety rather than treating it. (Source: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based)
source_refs: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based

options.text: Recommend a three-month trial of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy alone before considering any pharmacotherapy for either the ADHD or the concurrent generalised anxiety disorder
options.rationale: MBCT alone has weaker evidence than pharmacotherapy for moderate adult ADHD. Deferring pharmacotherapy for three months when both ADHD and moderate GAD are functionally impairing is not aligned with Australian evidence-based guidance. (Source: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based)
source_refs: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based

explanation.summary: The Australian ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline (AADPA, 2022) endorses stimulants (methylphenidate or dexamfetamine/lisdexamfetamine) as first-line pharmacotherapy for adult ADHD without contraindication. Common contraindications are uncontrolled cardiovascular disease, established arrhythmia, active psychotic illness and current substance use disorder. Comorbid anxiety is common and is not itself a contraindication; stimulant treatment can improve or worsen anxiety and needs monitoring during titration. Non-stimulant options (atomoxetine, guanfacine XR) are second line for stimulant failure or intolerance. CBT for comorbid GAD or depression is added rather than substituted. Treated ADHD reduces motor vehicle crash risk; the driving risk in adults with untreated ADHD is roughly double the general population.
key_points: Stimulants (methylphenidate, dexamfetamine, lisdexamfetamine) are first-line for adult ADHD.
Comorbid anxiety is not a stimulant contraindication; monitor during titration.
Treated ADHD improves rather than worsens driving safety.
Atomoxetine and guanfacine XR are second-line, especially with active substance use or contraindication.
Screen for cardiovascular risk (BP, personal or family arrhythmia/sudden death) before starting.
explanation.pearls: In adult ADHD with comorbid GAD, start immediate release methylphenidate at 5 mg twice daily and titrate every 1-2 weeks; add CBT for the anxiety - benzodiazepines and non-stimulants are second line.

sources.label: ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline - AADPA Australian evidence-based

subtopic_detail: Catatonia recognition and lorazepam challenge in a mixed presentation
stem:
You are the consult-liaison psychiatry registrar asked to see a 38 year old woman on the acute medical ward. She was admitted two days ago after being found by her sister mute and immobile in her lounge. She has a background of schizoaffective disorder on olanzapine 20 mg nightly for three years and was last well one week ago.

The medical team have excluded encephalitis (normal contrast CT brain, unremarkable MRI, normal CSF cell count and protein) and infection (afebrile, negative blood and urine cultures at 48 hours, unremarkable chest radiograph). Sodium, calcium, magnesium, thyroid function and creatinine are within normal limits. There is no history of neuroleptic dose change and creatine kinase is 220 U/L (30-160).

On examination she is awake with open eyes but does not track the examiner. She does not speak, will not obey command. When you raise her arm above her head she keeps it in that posture for over a minute. There is intermittent grimacing and echolalia when you speak softly.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: Screening positive with 5 features (immobility, mutism, staring, posturing, echolalia)
data_table.Investigations: CT and MRI brain unremarkable, CSF cell count and protein normal, sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), calcium corrected 2.30 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), CK 220 U/L (30-160), TSH 1.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase her olanzapine to 30 mg nightly and add haloperidol 5 mg intramuscularly every six hours as needed for agitation on the acute medical ward with continuous monitoring
options.rationale: Adding a further antipsychotic to a catatonic patient can precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome, especially in the setting of an already elevated creatine kinase. First-line treatment of catatonia is benzodiazepine, not more antipsychotic. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guideline)

options.text: Prescribe amantadine 100 mg orally twice daily as the first-line pharmacological therapy for catatonia because it has NMDA antagonism theoretically suitable for this presentation
options.rationale: Amantadine and memantine are third-line adjuncts for catatonia after benzodiazepine failure and ECT decision. Using it as first line is contrary to Australian and international guidance. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guideline)

options.text: Arrange emergency electroconvulsive therapy on the next available list without a benzodiazepine trial because catatonia unresponsive to olanzapine requires definitive immediate treatment
options.rationale: ECT is second-line for uncomplicated catatonia after a lorazepam trial and first-line only for malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis). Standard practice is to trial a benzodiazepine first; ECT is appropriate if the patient fails 24-72 hours of adequate lorazepam. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guideline)

options.text: Give a lorazepam 2 mg intramuscular challenge and reassess Bush-Francis at 30 minutes; if partial or full response, commence lorazepam 6 to 24 mg daily in divided doses
options.rationale: A positive lorazepam challenge (>=50% reduction in catatonic signs within an hour) is diagnostic and therapeutic. Standard care is subsequent lorazepam 6-24 mg daily in divided doses, with ECT reserved for malignant features or lorazepam failure at 72 hours. Antipsychotic dose adjustment is usually deferred until catatonia has cleared. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guideline)

options.text: Give intravenous midazolam 5 mg as the diagnostic challenge and repeat it every 30 minutes until she becomes responsive because midazolam has a faster onset time than lorazepam
options.rationale: Midazolam onset is faster but its short half-life makes it unsuitable for both diagnostic and therapeutic use in catatonia. The lorazepam challenge is the standardised test, and lorazepam is the therapeutic agent. Escalating midazolam risks respiratory depression without diagnostic clarity. (Source: RANZCP catatonia clinical guideline)

explanation.summary: Catatonia is under-recognised in general medical and psychiatric wards and is commonly triggered by mood or psychotic disorders (about 50%), general medical disease (autoimmune encephalitis, systemic lupus, sepsis, metabolic derangement) and medication effects. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale screens 14 signs (three positive features are enough to justify a challenge). The diagnostic and therapeutic gold standard is a lorazepam challenge (usually 2 mg IM or IV, reassessed at 30-60 minutes); a 50% or greater reduction in signs supports the diagnosis and is followed by 6-24 mg per day of lorazepam in divided doses. ECT is second-line for uncomplicated catatonia and first-line for malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis). Antipsychotic escalation risks precipitating NMS and is generally avoided until catatonia has cleared.
key_points: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale: 3 or more of 14 screening signs supports diagnosis.
First-line treatment is lorazepam challenge, then 6-24 mg/day in divided doses.
Malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rhabdomyolysis) is an ECT-first indication.
Antipsychotics can precipitate or worsen catatonia and are usually deferred until clearance.
Amantadine and memantine are third-line adjuncts.
explanation.pearls: A lorazepam challenge of 2 mg IM producing at least 50% reduction in Bush-Francis signs within an hour is both diagnostic and therapeutic - escalate to 6-24 mg/day in divided doses before considering ECT.

subtopic_detail: Serotonin syndrome versus neuroleptic malignant syndrome differentiation
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the emergency department to see a 42 year old woman brought in by her husband because of tremor, agitation and confusion beginning eight hours ago. She has treatment-resistant depression treated with sertraline 200 mg daily for two years. Nine days ago she was started on tranylcypromine 20 mg daily after a 14 day washout was recommended but the community psychiatrist agreed to a shorter overlap; her sertraline was tapered but not stopped. She took a single dose of tramadol 50 mg for dental pain twelve hours ago.

On examination she is tremulous, hyperreflexic with sustained clonus in both ankles more than the arms, dilated 5 mm reactive pupils, moist skin, and increased bowel sounds. Muscle tone is increased but not lead-pipe rigid; she can flex both elbows against resistance. She is oriented but restless.

Her venous blood gas is unremarkable, her creatinine is 74 micromol/L and creatine kinase is 380 U/L (30-160).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 178/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.4 degC
data_table.Neurology: Sustained ankle clonus, hyperreflexia lower more than upper, pupils dilated and reactive, tremor, moist skin, hyperactive bowel sounds, tone increased but non-rigid
data_table.Investigations: CK 380 U/L (30-160), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), venous blood gas pH 7.34 pCO2 40 lactate 2.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Load intravenous phenytoin 20 mg/kg for presumed status epilepticus and cool with a whole body ice pack until her core temperature falls below 37 degC before further investigation
options.rationale: There is no witnessed seizure and no epileptiform discharge; the clonus is myoclonic and reflex-driven, not epileptic. Whole-body ice pack cooling can trigger dangerous shivering; targeted cooling with active surface cooling and benzodiazepine sedation is the standard approach. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: serotonin toxicity)

options.text: Start intravenous bromocriptine 2.5 mg every eight hours plus oral dantrolene 1 mg/kg, admit to intensive care, and continue her sertraline unchanged given the depression relapse risk today
options.rationale: Bromocriptine and dantrolene are treatments for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not serotonin syndrome. The clinical features (clonus, hyperreflexia, dilated pupils, non-rigid hypertonia) point to serotonin syndrome. Continuing the offending serotonergic drug would worsen the clinical picture. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: serotonin toxicity)

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of haloperidol 5 mg to control her agitation, admit to a general medical ward, hold her sertraline for only 24 hours and restart it tomorrow morning
options.rationale: Antipsychotics may worsen thermodysregulation and add anticholinergic burden. Restarting sertraline within 24 hours re-exposes the patient to the offending combination. Cessation of all serotonergic drugs and specific supportive treatment is required. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: serotonin toxicity)

options.text: Stop all serotonergic drugs, transfer to a monitored bed, give intravenous fluids, sedate with benzodiazepines, and load cyproheptadine 12 mg then 2 mg every two hours if clonus persists
options.rationale: The lower-limb-dominant clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, moist skin and hyperactive bowel sounds distinguish this from NMS (lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, diaphoresis but no clonus, normal pupils). MAOI + SSRI + tramadol is a classic serotonin syndrome trigger. Treatment is drug cessation, benzodiazepine sedation, active cooling, and cyproheptadine as a serotonin 5HT2A antagonist. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: serotonin toxicity)

options.text: Give oral olanzapine 20 mg and transfer to a psychiatric acute unit for observation, holding her antidepressants until the on-call psychiatric team has been able to review her overnight
options.rationale: This is a medical emergency and requires management in an appropriately monitored medical environment, not on a psychiatric ward. Antipsychotics do not treat serotonin syndrome and olanzapine adds antihistaminergic and metabolic burden that will not help. (Source: eTG Complete Psychotropic: serotonin toxicity)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome (serotonin toxicity) develops within hours of a serotonergic combination or dose increase. Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria pivot on spontaneous or inducible clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, and hyperactive bowel sounds - typically with mydriasis. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome develops over days after antipsychotic exposure, features lead-pipe rigidity with hyporeflexia, altered mental state, autonomic instability, very high creatine kinase (often over 1000) and normal pupils. Management of serotonin syndrome is cessation of the trigger, IV fluids, benzodiazepine sedation, active surface cooling and, for moderate-to-severe cases, cyproheptadine 12 mg loading then 2 mg every two hours. Dantrolene and bromocriptine are the NMS-directed agents and are not used in serotonin toxicity.
key_points: Serotonin syndrome: clonus (esp. lower limb), hyperreflexia, mydriasis, hyperactive bowel sounds, moist skin.
NMS: lead-pipe rigidity, hyporeflexia, mental state change, autonomic instability, CK often > 1000.
MAOI + SSRI, SSRI + tramadol/linezolid, SSRI + triptan are classic serotonin syndrome triggers.
Treatment: stop trigger, fluids, benzodiazepines, active cooling; cyproheptadine for moderate/severe.
Bromocriptine and dantrolene treat NMS, NOT serotonin syndrome.
explanation.pearls: Sustained ankle clonus with mydriasis and hyperactive bowel sounds within hours of an MAOI-SSRI or SSRI-tramadol overlap is serotonin syndrome - give benzodiazepines, cool actively, and load cyproheptadine 12 mg then 2 mg every 2 hours.

subtopic_detail: Alcohol withdrawal with high seizure risk and CIWA-vs-fixed regimen choice
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 54 year old man to the acute medical ward. He drinks about 40 standard drinks a day for the last five years and his last drink was 30 hours ago. He was brought in by his brother after a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting 90 seconds; a similar seizure occurred during a previous inpatient detoxification two years ago.

In the emergency department he received IV thiamine 300 mg and IV diazepam 10 mg. He is now tremulous, diaphoretic, restless, oriented to person only, with a temperature of 38.1 degC. A creatine kinase is 1240 U/L (30-160), urea 8.4 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145) and magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1).

His CIWA-Ar score is 22. His prior detoxification failed with symptom-triggered dosing due to inconsistent assessment on a busy overnight shift; he progressed to delirium tremens on that admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 168/102 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.1 degC
data_table.Investigations: CK 1240 U/L (30-160), sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), glucose 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), ALT 92 U/L (<40), INR 1.4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Start symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar diazepam with hourly assessment on the general medical ward, replace magnesium and potassium, continue thiamine, and give haloperidol 5 mg IM as needed
options.rationale: Prior symptom-triggered dosing failed for this patient and produced delirium tremens. With active seizure history plus current severe withdrawal, RANZCP guidance recommends a fixed-schedule diazepam loading regimen (or combination with symptom-triggered top-ups) in a high-observation environment. Haloperidol lowers seizure threshold and should be avoided as first-line. (Source: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline

options.text: Load with intravenous phenytoin 20 mg/kg for seizure prophylaxis, restrict fluid to 800 mL a day for the hyponatraemia, and use oral oxazepam 30 mg only as needed for his agitation
options.rationale: Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures; benzodiazepines are the effective prophylaxis. Fluid restriction is inappropriate as the hyponatraemia is dilutional and may worsen with fluid restriction; correcting hypovolaemia and electrolytes safely is more appropriate. Oxazepam does not accumulate and is preferred in hepatic failure, but is under-dosing for a severe presentation. (Source: eTG Complete Addiction: alcohol withdrawal)

options.text: Load fixed diazepam 20 mg orally every two hours until CIWA-Ar <10 or sedation, admit to high dependency given prior withdrawal seizure, replace magnesium and give parenteral thiamine
options.rationale: Prior seizures during withdrawal plus current severe withdrawal (CIWA 22) plus recent seizure today classify this as very high risk. RANZCP endorses fixed diazepam loading (20 mg every two hours until CIWA <10 or sedation) in a HDU setting. Magnesium replacement below 0.7 mmol/L is standard because low magnesium prolongs withdrawal and worsens QT. Parenteral thiamine at 300 mg three times daily prevents Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline

options.text: Give a single intramuscular dose of olanzapine 10 mg with oral lorazepam 2 mg, then continue olanzapine 10 mg daily for the duration of the withdrawal to reduce his overall delirium risk
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not treat the underlying GABA-A receptor down-regulation of alcohol withdrawal and can lower seizure threshold. They are reserved for persistent psychotic symptoms after adequate benzodiazepine loading. Olanzapine does not substitute for a benzodiazepine load. (Source: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline)
source_refs: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline

options.text: Start acamprosate 666 mg three times daily and naltrexone 50 mg daily now, transfer to the addiction medicine consult service and observe on the general medical ward with hourly CIWA-Ar
options.rationale: Acamprosate and naltrexone are relapse prevention agents started after withdrawal is complete, not during acute withdrawal. Naltrexone specifically requires opioid abstinence and precipitates withdrawal if opioids present. Neither treats seizures or delirium tremens. (Source: eTG Complete Addiction: alcohol withdrawal)

explanation.summary: Acute alcohol withdrawal ranges from mild autonomic symptoms to delirium tremens (fever, autonomic instability, confusion, hallucinations, mortality up to 5% untreated). Prior withdrawal seizures and prior delirium tremens predict recurrence and drive management toward fixed-schedule benzodiazepine loading in a monitored setting. Diazepam has a long half-life and provides smoother taper; oxazepam is preferred in hepatic failure. Magnesium below 0.7 mmol/L is replaced because it prolongs withdrawal, increases seizure risk, and worsens QT prolongation. High-dose parenteral thiamine (300 mg three times daily for 3-5 days) prevents Wernicke encephalopathy - given IV or IM before any glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke. Antipsychotics are second-line, reserved for persistent psychosis after adequate sedation.
key_points: Fixed-schedule diazepam loading is preferred over symptom-triggered dosing when prior seizure or DT history.
Diazepam preferred for long half-life; oxazepam in hepatic failure.
Replace magnesium below 0.7 mmol/L to reduce seizure risk and prevent QT prolongation.
Parenteral thiamine 300 mg TDS for 3-5 days before any glucose to prevent Wernicke.
Naltrexone and acamprosate are relapse prevention agents started after withdrawal, not during.
explanation.pearls: Fixed diazepam load 20 mg every two hours until CIWA < 10 or sedation is the standard for severe alcohol withdrawal with a prior seizure history - magnesium replacement below 0.7 mmol/L and parenteral thiamine 300 mg TDS for 3-5 days round out the safe protocol.

sources.label: RANZCP alcohol withdrawal clinical practice guideline

subtopic_detail: Gamma-hydroxybutyrate withdrawal with autonomic instability and delirium
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar consulted in intensive care to see a 26 year old man who has become progressively agitated, diaphoretic and confused over the last 12 hours. He was admitted yesterday after a work injury and has been ventilated for the last 18 hours for an unrelated compartment syndrome. His partner has now disclosed daily 1,4-butanediol use ('G') dosed every 2 hours around the clock for the last 14 months, with his last dose approximately 22 hours ago.

The intensive care team have given diazepam 10 mg intravenously every two hours over the last six hours with only transient sedation, and lorazepam 4 mg intravenously two hours ago. He is currently tachycardic at 138, hypertensive at 195/108, hyperthermic at 39.1 degC, sweating profusely and pulling at his endotracheal tube; his RASS is +3. There are no focal neurological signs and CT brain is unremarkable. Blood cultures are pending and the septic workup is otherwise negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138 /min, blood pressure 195/108 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min ventilated, SpO2 98% on FiO2 0.35, temperature 39.1 degC
data_table.Sedation: Diazepam 10 mg IV every 2 hours x 3 (30 mg total) plus lorazepam 4 mg IV two hours ago, transient effect only, RASS +3
data_table.Investigations: CT brain unremarkable, sodium 141 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, magnesium 0.86 mmol/L, CK 640 U/L, blood cultures pending at 12 hours negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give propofol 100 microg/kg/min continuous infusion and dexmedetomidine 0.7 microg/kg/h with no further benzodiazepine or barbiturate, aiming for RASS -3 over the next 48 hours
options.rationale: Dexmedetomidine and propofol control autonomic and agitation symptoms but do not treat the underlying GABA receptor deficit and permit breakthrough seizures and cardiovascular instability on weaning. They are adjuncts to, not substitutes for, GABAergic loading. (Source: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline

options.text: Stop all benzodiazepines because they are ineffective, and give a single intramuscular dose of haloperidol 10 mg plus olanzapine 10 mg via nasogastric tube for control of agitation now
options.rationale: Antipsychotic monotherapy in GHB withdrawal without an underlying benzodiazepine backbone is dangerous - it lowers seizure threshold, worsens hyperthermia, and does not treat the GABAergic receptor down-regulation that is driving symptoms. Benzodiazepines remain part of the regimen, with barbiturate or GHB replacement added. (Source: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline

options.text: Change to high-dose IV midazolam infusion at 0.5 mg/kg/h, add phenobarbitone loading 5 mg/kg then 2 mg/kg every 4 hours to a level of 25-40 mg/L, and consider sodium oxybate bridging
options.rationale: GHB and its prodrug 1,4-butanediol act largely through GABA-B receptors, so benzodiazepine monotherapy is frequently insufficient - the ceiling reported in case series is often above 200 mg diazepam-equivalent per day. Phenobarbitone acts at GABA-A independently of the benzodiazepine site and augments control; sodium oxybate substitution under specialist supervision provides a pharmaceutical taper. Ongoing intensive care and cooling are required. (Source: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline

options.text: Load flumazenil 0.2 mg intravenously and repeat as needed to reverse the accumulated benzodiazepines because they are contributing to his delirium and treatment-resistant agitation
options.rationale: Flumazenil in a benzodiazepine-tolerant patient precipitates seizures and worsens withdrawal. It has no role in managing withdrawal, and the current problem is inadequate GABAergic coverage, not benzodiazepine excess. (Source: eTG Complete Toxicology: benzodiazepine toxicity)

options.text: Start baclofen 20 mg via nasogastric tube every eight hours as the sole treatment because it is a GABA-B agonist that mimics GHB and will control his withdrawal symptoms adequately
options.rationale: Baclofen has a role in GHB withdrawal as an adjunct given its GABA-B agonism, but baclofen monotherapy is inadequate for severe autonomic instability. It is used in combination with titrated benzodiazepine and barbiturate loading, and toxicity itself can produce delirium and coma. (Source: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline)
source_refs: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline

explanation.summary: GHB and its prodrug 1,4-butanediol produce dose-dependent GABA-B receptor activation with a secondary GABA-A effect. Regular around-the-clock dosing over months down-regulates both pathways, so withdrawal can begin within hours of cessation and progress to a life-threatening syndrome that includes severe autonomic instability, delirium, psychosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and seizures. Because the primary receptor target differs from alcohol and benzodiazepines, benzodiazepine monotherapy is often inadequate and case series report requirements above 200 mg diazepam-equivalent per day. NSW Health and the RACP addiction medicine consensus support intensive care admission for severe cases, high-dose benzodiazepine infusion plus phenobarbitone loading (to a level of 25-40 mg/L), and pharmaceutical GHB (sodium oxybate) substitution under specialist supervision. Baclofen and dexmedetomidine are adjuncts.
key_points: GHB/1,4-BD act primarily at GABA-B; benzodiazepine monotherapy is often inadequate.
Onset within hours of cessation; severe cases progress within 24 hours.
Phenobarbitone loading is standard adjunct (target 25-40 mg/L) via GABA-A independent of benzodiazepine site.
Sodium oxybate substitution under addiction medicine supervision provides a pharmaceutical taper.
Baclofen and dexmedetomidine are adjuncts, not monotherapy.
explanation.pearls: Around-the-clock GHB or 1,4-BD dependence needs intensive care admission with high-dose benzodiazepine plus phenobarbitone loading to a level of 25-40 mg/L, not benzodiazepine monotherapy - benzodiazepines act at GABA-A and GHB's dominant target is GABA-B.

sources.label: NSW Health GHB and 1,4-BD dependence and withdrawal guideline

subtopic_detail: Acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy - antibiotic selection
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 28 year old woman at 24 plus 2 weeks gestation who presents to the emergency department with a 24 hour history of right loin pain, rigors and vomiting. Her first pregnancy is otherwise progressing normally with a booking booking eGFR of 118 mL/min/1.73 m^2. She has no allergies.

She reports dysuria and increased urinary frequency for four days. She has been drinking about 500 mL of cranberry juice daily on advice from a friend. There is no vaginal loss, no contractions and normal foetal movements on maternal report.

On examination she is uncomfortable, tender in the right renal angle with guarding, temperature 39.0 degC, pulse 118, blood pressure 108/64. Urine dipstick shows 3+ blood, 3+ nitrites and 3+ leukocytes; a urine culture and blood cultures have been sent. Foetal heart rate is 154 with reactive traces on CTG.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.0 degC, foetal heart rate 154 /min
data_table.Examination: Right renal angle tenderness with guarding, no peritonism, no vaginal loss, uterus soft, no contractions palpable
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick 3+ blood 3+ nitrites 3+ leukocytes; venous lactate 2.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); creatinine 58 micromol/L (booking eGFR 118); CTG reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times a day for ten days with early general practice review at 48 hours and observation for symptom progression during that period at home if needed
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are inappropriate for a woman with pyelonephritis in pregnancy who is systemically unwell with vomiting; poor absorption from vomiting undermines efficacy and misses septic complications. Admission for IV therapy is the standard. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for seven days with instructions to return to the emergency department if her symptoms worsen or if she develops any new pregnancy concerns
options.rationale: Trimethoprim is contraindicated in the first trimester and cautioned throughout pregnancy because of folate antagonism. It is not adequate monotherapy for pyelonephritis and is not the correct empirical agent. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

options.text: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily plus IV amoxicillin 2 g every six hours for seven days then oral amoxicillin to complete a total of fourteen days of antibiotic treatment
options.rationale: Gentamicin is reserved for severe sepsis or when a resistant organism is documented in pregnancy given the fetal ototoxicity concerns. It is not the routine first-line agent for straightforward pyelonephritis in pregnancy when a cephalosporin is appropriate. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily until clinical improvement then step down to oral cefalexin per susceptibility, for a total of ten to fourteen days of antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: First-line empirical therapy for pyelonephritis in pregnancy per eTG Complete is IV cefazolin OR IV ceftriaxone with step-down to an oral cephalosporin per susceptibility. Ceftriaxone once daily is a convenient equivalent, well studied in pregnancy, and covers the usual E coli spectrum. Total duration ten to fourteen days. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

options.text: Oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for five days then a two-week repeat urine culture to confirm eradication of the underlying urinary tract infection organism at home
options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin achieves urinary but not renal tissue concentrations sufficient to treat pyelonephritis; it is a cystitis-only agent. It also should be avoided at term because of haemolysis risk in the neonate. (Source: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy)
source_refs: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pyelonephritis complicates approximately 1-2% of pregnancies and carries important obstetric consequences: septic shock, preterm labour and adult respiratory distress syndrome. Admission for IV antibiotics, adequate hydration and fetal monitoring is standard. Empirical therapy per eTG Complete is IV cefazolin 2 g eight-hourly OR IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily, with step-down to an oral cephalosporin per culture and sensitivity; total course is 10-14 days. Gentamicin is reserved for severe sepsis or for cephalosporin failure. Trimethoprim (folate antagonism, first trimester) and nitrofurantoin (neonatal haemolysis at term, poor tissue penetration) are cystitis-only agents. Follow-up urine culture is standard to confirm eradication.
key_points: IV cefazolin or ceftriaxone is first-line empirical pyelonephritis therapy in pregnancy.
Step down to oral cephalosporin per susceptibility for a total 10-14 day course.
Nitrofurantoin does NOT treat pyelonephritis (renal tissue penetration inadequate).
Trimethoprim contraindicated first trimester; nitrofurantoin avoided at term.
Follow-up culture confirms eradication; consider suppressive antibiotic if recurrence.
explanation.pearls: For pyelonephritis at 24 weeks, admit for IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily and step down to oral cefalexin per susceptibility for a total ten to fourteen day course - nitrofurantoin never treats pyelonephritis.

sources.label: eTG Complete Antibiotic: pyelonephritis in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Migraine preventive selection in a patient with prior ischaemic stroke
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 44 year old woman in your clinic. She has had episodic migraine with aura since her teens. Over the last four months her attacks have increased to about six per month, each lasting a day. She uses sumatriptan 50 mg per attack with good relief.

Two years ago she had a small right occipital ischaemic stroke; magnetic resonance angiography showed no arterial abnormality. She was subsequently found to have a patent foramen ovale which was closed percutaneously and she is on aspirin 100 mg daily. Her blood pressure has been reliably 132/82. She is not planning pregnancy.

Her body mass index is 24 kg/m^2. She has no depression, no history of asthma, no history of Raynaud, and no orthostatic symptoms. Her PHQ-9 is 3.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68 /min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Neurology: Cranial nerves intact, no field defect on confrontation, normal cerebellar and long-tract examination
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg daily; sumatriptan 50 mg as needed (about 6 tablets per month)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line preventive medication?

options.text: Continue combined oral contraceptive-based hormonal manipulation with a low dose norethisterone-only regimen for cycle-linked prophylaxis against her recurrent migraine
options.rationale: Combined hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated in migraine with aura because of the additional stroke risk. This patient already has a documented ischaemic stroke and a PFO; starting oestrogen-containing agents is unsafe. Progestogen-only regimens are not established migraine prophylaxis. (Source: eTG Complete Sexual health: contraception in migraine)
source_refs: eTG Complete Sexual health: contraception in migraine

options.text: Amitriptyline 10 mg at night up-titrating to 75 mg over eight weeks, plus vitamin B2 riboflavin 400 mg daily and magnesium oxide 600 mg daily as adjunctive prevention
options.rationale: Amitriptyline is a legitimate second-line preventive but its anticholinergic burden, orthostatic hypotension risk and weight gain make it less desirable when a beta blocker is well tolerated. Riboflavin and magnesium have modest evidence and should not replace evidence-based first-line agents. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology: migraine prevention)

options.text: Topiramate 25 mg at night titrating to 100 mg per day in divided doses, aiming for at least a twelve-week trial before assessing her response to preventive treatment
options.rationale: Topiramate is an alternative first-line preventive but has cognitive slowing, paraesthesiae, renal stones and teratogenicity concerns that make propranolol a better default when there is no contraindication. Not clearly superior in this patient. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology: migraine prevention)

options.text: Verapamil sustained release 240 mg daily as first-line preventive because it addresses cortical spreading depression and has a favourable cardiovascular safety profile
options.rationale: Verapamil is first line for cluster headache, not migraine prevention. Australian guidance places it much lower in the migraine preventive hierarchy and there is no reason to preference it here. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology: migraine prevention)

options.text: Propranolol 20 mg twice daily up-titrating to 40 mg twice daily as tolerated, aiming for at least an eight-week trial before assessing her response to preventive therapy
options.rationale: Propranolol is a first-line migraine preventive with the best evidence base in Australia and is well tolerated at 40-160 mg per day. It is not contraindicated by a prior ischaemic stroke in the absence of significant conduction disease. Its neutral cardiovascular profile suits secondary stroke prevention. (Source: eTG Complete Neurology: migraine prevention)

explanation.summary: Migraine prevention is offered when attacks are frequent (three or more per month), disabling, or acute treatments are inadequate or overused. Australian first-line agents are propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, candesartan, and pizotifen; CGRP-targeted monoclonal antibodies are reserved for treatment-refractory disease with public subsidy criteria. Selection is driven by comorbidity: hypertension favours propranolol or candesartan; depression favours amitriptyline; epilepsy or obesity favours topiramate; contraception planning favours candesartan or propranolol. Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated in migraine with aura because of stroke risk. Triptans are contraindicated in ischaemic vascular disease and uncontrolled hypertension; this woman's triptan use should be reviewed with a neurologist.
key_points: Preventive threshold: three or more disabling attacks per month, or inadequate acute treatment.
First-line Australian agents: propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, candesartan, pizotifen.
Combined hormonal contraception contraindicated in migraine with aura (stroke risk).
Triptans contraindicated in ischaemic vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension.
CGRP monoclonal antibodies are treatment refractory second/third line under PBS criteria.
explanation.pearls: In migraine with aura and a prior ischaemic stroke, first line prevention is propranolol 40-160 mg per day and combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated - review the triptan too, because triptans should be avoided after ischaemic stroke.

sources.label: eTG Complete Sexual health: contraception in migraine

subtopic_detail: IV iron indication after oral failure in inflammatory bowel disease
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 32 year old man with ulcerative colitis on mesalazine 3 g daily. He is currently in clinical remission with a Simple Clinical Colitis Activity Index of 1 and his last calprotectin six weeks ago was 92 microg/g (>250 suggests active disease).

Three months ago iron deficiency anaemia was diagnosed and he was started on ferrous sulfate 325 mg (105 mg elemental iron) three times a day. He tolerated this for four weeks then developed severe cramping abdominal pain and nausea; he stopped tablets after eight weeks and repeat FBC today shows persistent microcytic anaemia. He denies overt bleeding and stools remain formed.

He has no cardiovascular disease. He is not planning international travel in the next month. Weight is 72 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Full blood count: Haemoglobin 102 g/L (135-180), MCV 74 fL (80-100), MCH 25 pg (27-34), platelets 428 x10^9/L (150-400), reticulocytes 65 x10^9/L (25-100)
data_table.Iron studies: Ferritin 8 microg/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 8% (>16), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), calprotectin 92 microg/g
data_table.Other: Coeliac serology negative, TSH 1.6 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial an alternative oral iron preparation using ferrous fumarate 210 mg (68 mg elemental) once daily on alternate days for eight weeks and repeat the full blood count
options.rationale: Alternate-day oral iron reduces gastrointestinal side effects and improves absorption in some patients, but a substantial GI intolerance history in active or previously active IBD is a recognised indication for switching to IV iron rather than a further oral trial. (Source: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement)
source_refs: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement

options.text: Arrange a two unit packed red blood cell transfusion this week to correct the anaemia and start ferric carboxymaltose only after the haemoglobin exceeds 120 g/L
options.rationale: Packed red cell transfusion is reserved for symptomatic anaemia, haemodynamic instability, or very low haemoglobin (typically below 70 g/L outside cardiovascular disease). This patient is haemodynamically stable at 102 g/L and IV iron alone will address the deficit safely. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)

options.text: Arrange four weekly intramuscular iron polymaltose 250 mg injections in the general practice clinic to total 1000 mg of parenteral elemental iron replacement therapy
options.rationale: Intramuscular iron produces persistent painful skin staining, unreliable absorption and inferior haematological response compared with IV iron. It is no longer recommended and is not offered in current Australian practice. (Source: AMH: iron preparations)

options.text: Refer for elective total colectomy given the iron deficiency represents ongoing occult blood loss from the colon despite adherent mesalazine dosing over the past year
options.rationale: There is no evidence of active disease (calprotectin 92, SCCAI 1, no visible bleeding). Colectomy is not indicated by iron deficiency alone in an otherwise remitting patient. Iron deficiency in IBD often reflects reduced absorption and chronic inflammation rather than ongoing loss. (Source: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement)
source_refs: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement

options.text: Arrange intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes as a single-dose replacement, with a repeat ferritin and full blood count planned in eight weeks
options.rationale: GESA endorses IV iron as first line in iron deficiency anaemia complicating IBD when oral iron is not tolerated, ineffective, or during active disease. Ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg as a single infusion is standard for a 72 kg patient with haemoglobin 102 g/L; repeat FBC and ferritin at eight weeks assesses response and stores. (Source: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement)
source_refs: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency anaemia affects up to a third of patients with inflammatory bowel disease and is multifactorial: chronic blood loss, chronic inflammation reducing absorption via elevated hepcidin, and oral iron intolerance. The Gastroenterological Society of Australia endorses IV iron as first line in IBD when oral iron is not tolerated, ineffective, or during active disease. Ferric carboxymaltose (1000 mg per infusion, maximum single dose 15 mg/kg or 1000 mg) and iron polymaltose (slower infusion) are the available preparations. Total dose is calculated by the Ganzoni formula or the simplified fixed-dose approach; a 1000 mg dose typically replenishes stores in a 60-90 kg adult with moderate anaemia. Response is assessed at eight weeks with FBC and ferritin. Transfusion is reserved for symptomatic severe anaemia.
key_points: IV iron is first-line for iron deficiency in IBD if oral not tolerated, ineffective, or active disease.
Ferric carboxymaltose maximum single dose 15 mg/kg or 1000 mg per infusion.
IM iron is no longer recommended (staining, poor absorption).
Reassess FBC and ferritin at eight weeks after infusion.
Watch for post-infusion hypophosphataemia (ferric carboxymaltose specific).
explanation.pearls: For iron deficiency in IBD with oral iron intolerance, use IV ferric carboxymaltose 1000 mg over 15 minutes and reassess FBC and ferritin at eight weeks - watch for hypophosphataemia specific to ferric carboxymaltose.

sources.label: GESA Iron deficiency in IBD position statement

subtopic_detail: Denosumab discontinuation and the rebound vertebral fracture window
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 71 year old woman in your clinic. She has had postmenopausal osteoporosis on subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg six-monthly for the last four years. Her most recent dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry scan reported an L1-L4 T-score of -1.6 and a total hip T-score of -2.2. She had a wrist fracture ten years ago after a fall from standing.

She now wishes to stop denosumab, having read that it does not need to be continued indefinitely. Her creatinine clearance is 62 mL/min, her serum calcium is 2.36 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), she has no history of hypocalcaemia, no history of dental extraction planned in the next year, and no history of jaw pain.

Her next denosumab dose is due in three weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Bone density: L1-L4 T-score -1.6, total hip T-score -2.2, femoral neck T-score -2.4
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.36 mmol/L (2.15-2.55), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.75-1.5), 25-OH vitamin D 78 nmol/L (>50), eGFR 62 mL/min/1.73 m^2, PTH 4.2 pmol/L (1.6-6.9)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan for discontinuing denosumab?

options.text: Continue denosumab indefinitely because discontinuation carries a substantial rebound vertebral fracture risk that cannot be mitigated safely with any current bone-antiresorptive agent
options.rationale: Discontinuation is legitimate provided the transition is managed. Indefinite denosumab in a patient in the osteopenic range (hip T-score -2.2, spine -1.6 on treatment) after four years without fracture is not mandated; the risk lies in stopping without a bone-antiresorptive hand-over. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis: prevention, diagnosis and management)
source_refs: RACGP Osteoporosis: prevention, diagnosis and management

options.text: Skip the next scheduled denosumab dose and observe with three-monthly clinical review and annual DXA scans, adding calcium 1200 mg and vitamin D 1000 IU supplementation daily
options.rationale: Simply stopping denosumab without bisphosphonate cover produces rebound multiple vertebral fractures typically 8-18 months later, with reports of six or more concurrent vertebral fractures at re-presentation. Observation and supplements do not mitigate this. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement

options.text: Give the next scheduled denosumab dose on time, then transition to a single dose of zoledronic acid 5 mg IV six months later, with plans to repeat DXA at 12-24 months
options.rationale: Discontinuation of denosumab is followed within 6-9 months by a rebound in bone remodelling with documented multiple vertebral fractures. Endocrine Society of Australia and Osteoporosis Australia endorse a bisphosphonate hand-over: continue on-time denosumab dosing until the transition, then give zoledronic acid IV at the time the next denosumab dose would have been due. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement
RACGP Osteoporosis: prevention, diagnosis and management

options.text: Switch immediately to teriparatide 20 microg subcutaneously daily for 18 months as the anabolic agent of choice after denosumab, with no bisphosphonate cover during that period
options.rationale: Teriparatide after denosumab is associated with accelerated bone loss at the hip in the first year and does not prevent the rebound resorption of denosumab discontinuation. It is not the correct sequence; teriparatide is best used before denosumab or bisphosphonate. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement

options.text: Continue calcium supplementation only and repeat DXA at 24 months, planning to intervene only if the T-score deteriorates by more than 0.5 standard deviation from current levels
options.rationale: DXA decline lags the rebound resorption by many months and the fractures often occur before a detectable T-score drop. Waiting for imaging change misses the therapeutic window; hand-over antiresorptive is planned at the time of the missed dose. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement

explanation.summary: Denosumab is a RANKL inhibitor whose bone effect reverses rapidly on cessation because it does not embed in bone. Discontinuation without a bisphosphonate hand-over causes a rebound in bone remodelling with reported multiple vertebral fractures 8-18 months after the last dose. Australian endocrine consensus is to continue denosumab dosing on schedule and give a single dose of intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg six months after the last denosumab dose, at the time the next injection would have been due. Repeat DXA and consider a second zoledronic acid dose at 12-24 months based on bone turnover markers and DXA. Oral bisphosphonates (alendronate 70 mg weekly) are an alternative if IV administration is impractical, though evidence is stronger for the IV route. Calcium, vitamin D sufficiency and fall prevention support any regimen.
key_points: Denosumab effect reverses rapidly on cessation because it does not embed in bone.
Multiple vertebral fractures 8-18 months after last dose are reported without hand-over.
Standard hand-over: zoledronic acid 5 mg IV at the time the next denosumab dose was due.
Alendronate 70 mg weekly is an alternative when IV is impractical.
Teriparatide after denosumab is associated with accelerated hip bone loss in the first year.
explanation.pearls: When stopping denosumab, give a single dose of IV zoledronic acid 5 mg six months after the last denosumab dose, at the time the next injection was due - waiting for DXA decline before intervening misses the rebound vertebral fracture window.

sources.label: RACGP Osteoporosis: prevention, diagnosis and management
Endocrine Society of Australia denosumab discontinuation statement

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis in known primary adrenal insufficiency triggered by gastroenteritis
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 38 year old woman with known primary adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking, 10 mg lunchtime, 5 mg late afternoon plus fludrocortisone 100 microg daily. She has been vomiting and passing watery diarrhoea for 24 hours after a family gathering, and has been unable to keep her tablets down since 6 am today.

She is drowsy but rousable, cool peripherally, with dry mucous membranes and normal glucose. There is no abdominal peritonism and no fever above 37.6 degC. She has been taking her medical alert card and a hydrocortisone emergency injection kit but did not use them because she 'didn't feel that bad'.

Her point-of-care venous gas shows a metabolic acidosis with a bicarbonate of 16 mmol/L. Sodium is 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, glucose 3.9 mmol/L, and creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 68).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.4 degC
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 68), VBG pH 7.28 pCO2 32 HCO3 16 lactate 3.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2)
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20/10/5 mg daily oral; fludrocortisone 100 microg daily oral; emergency intramuscular hydrocortisone kit in her bag, unused

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus and increase her oral hydrocortisone to 40 mg every six hours, waiting until she can keep tablets down before considering any further intervention
options.rationale: Oral hydrocortisone cannot be relied on in an actively vomiting patient in adrenal crisis. Delay in giving IV or IM hydrocortisone is directly associated with mortality. Fluid resuscitation is correct but must be paired with immediate parenteral glucocorticoid. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

options.text: Prioritise potassium reduction with calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% intravenously, insulin-dextrose infusion and salbutamol nebulisation before any glucocorticoid because the hyperkalaemia is the immediate life threat
options.rationale: Potassium of 5.8 mmol/L without significant ECG change (no wide QRS, no peaked T waves in this vignette) is not the immediate life threat; the hypovolaemic shock and cortisol deficiency are. IV hydrocortisone and saline correct both the hyperkalaemia (via mineralocorticoid effect and volume) and the shock. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

options.text: Give dexamethasone 8 mg intravenously as the first-line agent because it has minimal mineralocorticoid effect and does not confound subsequent short synacthen testing for adrenal insufficiency
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is second choice when the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency is not yet made and short synacthen testing is planned. In known Addison disease with adrenal crisis, hydrocortisone is preferred because of its mineralocorticoid activity at high dose and long clinical experience. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

options.text: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM immediately, follow with 1 L normal saline over the first hour, continue hydrocortisone 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion, and admit for observation
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis in a woman with a gastroenteritis trigger who cannot absorb oral therapy needs immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg followed by 200 mg per 24 hours (as a continuous infusion or 50 mg every 6 hours) plus aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation. Fludrocortisone is unnecessary at these hydrocortisone doses because they saturate mineralocorticoid receptors. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

options.text: Load intravenous 3% saline for the hyponatraemia targeting a rise of 6 mmol/L over the first hour, and delay giving hydrocortisone until her serum sodium has corrected to 130 mmol/L
options.rationale: The hyponatraemia is hypovolaemic and cortisol-deficiency related and resolves with isotonic saline and hydrocortisone. Rapid correction with hypertonic saline in this setting increases the risk of osmotic demyelination. Delaying hydrocortisone is dangerous. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis in known primary adrenal insufficiency is precipitated by infection (most commonly gastroenteritis), surgery, trauma or physical stress; mortality is 6% per crisis and higher when steroid delivery is delayed. Diagnosis is clinical: hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, prerenal acute kidney injury, non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Treatment is immediate IV or IM hydrocortisone 100 mg followed by 200 mg per 24 hours as continuous infusion or 50 mg every six hours, plus rapid isotonic fluid resuscitation. Fludrocortisone is not needed while hydrocortisone dose is above 40-50 mg per day because mineralocorticoid receptors are saturated. Patient education on sick-day rules (double or triple oral dose for fever, IM hydrocortisone for vomiting) prevents recurrence.
key_points: Adrenal crisis = hypotension + hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia + hypoglycaemia + prerenal AKI in known Addison.
First step: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV or IM (not oral, not delayed), then 200 mg per 24 hours.
Isotonic saline resuscitation restores volume and corrects hyponatraemia safely.
Fludrocortisone not needed while hydrocortisone above 40-50 mg per day.
Sick-day rules: double or triple oral dose for fever; IM hydrocortisone if vomiting.
explanation.pearls: In known Addison disease with vomiting, give IM or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately then 200 mg per 24 hours - waiting to see if she can keep oral tablets down is where adrenal crisis mortality happens.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guideline

subtopic_detail: Clinically isolated syndrome and application of McDonald 2017 criteria
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman referred by her general practitioner with a first episode of blurred central vision in her right eye that developed over three days and is improving over the last two weeks. She reports pain on eye movement during the acute phase. She has no past medical history and takes no medications.

On examination her right visual acuity is 6/12 improving from 6/24, colour desaturation on Ishihara plates, a right relative afferent pupillary defect, and normal fundoscopy. The rest of the neurological examination is normal. Ophthalmology has confirmed optic neuritis.

MRI brain with contrast reports two ovoid periventricular T2 hyperintense lesions and one juxtacortical lesion, one of which enhances with gadolinium. Spinal MRI is normal. CSF shows two oligoclonal bands unique to CSF and no white cells. Serum aquaporin-4 IgG and MOG-IgG are negative. Standard MS mimics (Lyme serology, B12, TSH, syphilis, HIV) are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Ophthalmology: Right visual acuity 6/12 (improving), colour desaturation, right RAPD, normal fundoscopy
data_table.MRI brain: 2 periventricular T2 lesions, 1 juxtacortical T2 lesion, 1 lesion enhances with gadolinium
data_table.CSF and serology: CSF 2 oligoclonal bands unique to CSF, no cells; aquaporin-4 IgG negative; MOG-IgG negative; TPHA, HIV, B12, TSH normal

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose clinically isolated syndrome and defer any diagnosis of multiple sclerosis; re-image at three months and reassess for dissemination in time only at that scheduled follow-up
options.rationale: Under McDonald 2017 criteria, dissemination in space AND time can both be met on a single scan when both enhancing and non-enhancing lesions coexist. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time in the setting of dissemination in space. This patient meets MS criteria now. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria for MS diagnosis)

options.text: Start high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for five days followed by an oral prednisolone taper as monotherapy without any specific multiple sclerosis directed therapy
options.rationale: IV methylprednisolone shortens the optic neuritis relapse duration but does not alter the natural history of MS. Recognising she meets MS criteria and referring for disease-modifying therapy is what changes long-term outcomes. Corticosteroid alone is insufficient. (Source: MS Society Australia clinical guideline)

options.text: Treat as neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder empirically with monthly intravenous rituximab because optic neuritis plus white matter lesions represents a high-risk demyelinating phenotype
options.rationale: Aquaporin-4 IgG is negative and MOG-IgG is negative; the imaging pattern is not typical of NMOSD (NMOSD usually shows longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis and area postrema lesions). Empirical rituximab commits to a costly and immunosuppressive regimen for the wrong disease. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria for MS diagnosis)

options.text: Confirm the diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis on 2017 McDonald criteria today and refer urgently to a neurologist for disease-modifying therapy discussion this week
options.rationale: Optic neuritis plus periventricular and juxtacortical lesions provides dissemination in space; the coexistence of enhancing and non-enhancing lesions provides dissemination in time. CSF-specific oligoclonal bands provide an additional route to dissemination in time in the 2017 revision. Early DMT reduces long-term disability. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria for MS diagnosis)

options.text: Arrange a lumbar puncture to measure JCV serology and a MOG-IgG titre before making any diagnosis of demyelinating disease that could commit her to lifelong disease-modifying therapy
options.rationale: MOG-IgG and JCV are relevant to differential diagnosis and monitoring, but MOG-IgG is already negative on the vignette and JCV serology is used to stratify natalizumab progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy risk, not to make an MS diagnosis. Delaying diagnosis for these is not indicated. (Source: 2017 McDonald criteria for MS diagnosis)

explanation.summary: The 2017 revision of the McDonald criteria allows a diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis after a first clinical attack (a clinically isolated syndrome) when MRI shows dissemination in space (T2 lesions in at least two of four typical locations: periventricular, juxtacortical or cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord) and dissemination in time (the simultaneous presence of enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the same scan, OR a new T2 or gadolinium-enhancing lesion on a follow-up scan). CSF-specific oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time when dissemination in space is fulfilled. Early disease-modifying therapy reduces long-term relapse rate and disability accrual. Australian first-line DMTs include glatiramer acetate, interferon beta and dimethyl fumarate; higher-efficacy options include fingolimod, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab and natalizumab, chosen with the neurology team.
key_points: McDonald 2017: dissemination in space in 2 of 4 typical locations plus DIT.
DIT is met by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, new lesion on follow-up MRI, or CSF-specific oligoclonal bands.
Aquaporin-4 IgG for NMOSD; MOG-IgG for MOG-antibody disease - both differentials to exclude.
IV methylprednisolone shortens relapse duration but does not alter MS natural history.
Early DMT reduces long-term relapse rate and disability accrual.
explanation.pearls: A first optic neuritis with periventricular plus juxtacortical lesions and CSF-specific oligoclonal bands meets 2017 McDonald criteria today - bands substitute for dissemination in time and start the clock on disease-modifying therapy.

subtopic_detail: Acute HIV seroconversion in the acute retroviral syndrome window
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 24 year old man with a two week history of fever, sore throat, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, arthralgia and a non-pruritic maculopapular rash on his trunk. He reports condomless receptive anal sex with a casual male partner four weeks ago in Melbourne and has not started HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis.
